% A minipage cannot break across leaves: it overruns in silence. So every unit is
% boxed, its height written out, and only then set — python compares the height
% against \textheight. This is the measurement the mirror got from page marks.
\newcommand{\originals}[3]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\noindent
    \begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
      \footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}\plreset\plnumtrue #2
    \end{minipage}\hfill
    \begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
      \footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}\plreset\plnumtrue
      \setnoted{}#3
    \end{minipage}\par}%
  % ⚠ \ht0 ALONE IS WRONG HERE and silently reported ~5.7pt for every Part I
  % verso until 2026-08-09. This vbox's content is ONE LINE of two tall boxes, so
  % its height is just that line's height above the baseline and the whole column
  % sits in the DEPTH. Measure ht+dp. (\originalsone and \enleaf are multi-line
  % vboxes and were never affected.)
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H O #1 \the\dimexpr\ht0+\dp0\relax}\box0}

\newcommand{\originalsone}[3]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}\plreset\plnumtrue #2}%
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H O #1 \the\ht0}%
  \ifthenelse{\equal{#3}{epigraph}}{\dropto{0.16}\box0}{\box0}}

\newcommand{\enleaf}[3]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\small\plreset\plnumtrue #2}%
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H E #1 \the\ht0}%
  \ifthenelse{\equal{#3}{epigraph}}{\dropto{0.16}\box0}{\box0}}

% ---- the two foot-bands -------------------------------------------------
% The Loeb leaves roughly 44% of every leaf empty, and a Loeb's foot is where an
% apparatus belongs. The verso band carries the apparatus criticus against the
% originals; the recto band carries explanatory notes against the English.
%
% ⚠ The band is set at the FOOT, which means the leaf must be composed as a box
% of exactly \textheight with \vfill between body and band. \vfil alone will not
% do it: the preamble sets \raggedbottom, whose own bottom glue competes with it
% and lands the band a third of the way up. Same trap as the display leaves.
%
% ⚠ The band is measured INTO the fit record (\dimexpr body + band), not beside
% it. A band that overruns is exactly as silent as a minipage that overruns, and
% the point of the instrument is that nothing is unmeasured — which is how Part
% I's verso went 131 leaves without ever being tested.
% ⚠ The \par after the rule is load-bearing: without it the rule is just an inline
% box and the band's first word sets on the same line as the rule.
\newcommand{\bandrule}{\par\vspace{5pt}%
  {\noindent\color{rulegray}\rule{0.28\textwidth}{0.4pt}\par}\vspace{3.5pt}}

\newcommand{\apparatusband}[1]{%
  \bandrule{\scriptsize\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}\setlength{\parskip}{1pt}%
    \raggedright #1\par}}

\newcommand{\notesband}[1]{%
  \bandrule{\footnotesize\setlength{\parindent}{0pt}\setlength{\parskip}{2pt}%
    #1\par}}

% Compose a leaf whose body sits at the top and whose band sits at the foot.
\newcommand{\bandleaf}[2]{\vbox to \textheight{#1\vfill#2}}

% #5 = the Latin column's own noted lines, #6 = how many romans the Greek column
% already spent, so the series runs on rather than restarting at i.
\newcommand{\originalsn}[6]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\noindent
    \begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
      \footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}\plreset\plnumtrue #2
    \end{minipage}\hfill
    \begin{minipage}[t]{0.485\textwidth}
      % ⚠ numbered on ITS OWN count — see the preamble. It is NOT reliably
      % line-for-line with the Greek: 20 of Part I's 131 openings differ, by as
      % much as six lines, because the plate turns its own long lines.
      \footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}%
      \setnotedcol{#5}{#6}\plreset\plnumtrue #3
    \end{minipage}\par}%
  \setbox2=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\apparatusband{#4}}%
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H O #1 \the\dimexpr\ht0+\dp0+\ht2+\dp2\relax}%
  \bandleaf{\box0}{\box2}}

\newcommand{\originalsonen}[4]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\footnotesize\setlength{\plhang}{1.5em}\plreset\plnumtrue #2}%
  \setbox2=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\apparatusband{#4}}%
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H O #1 \the\dimexpr\ht0+\ht2+\dp2\relax}%
  \bandleaf{\box0}{\box2}}

\newcommand{\enleafn}[4]{%
  \setbox0=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\small\plreset\plnumtrue #2}%
  \setbox2=\vbox{\hsize=\textwidth\notesband{#4}}%
  \immediate\write\fitfile{H E #1 \the\dimexpr\ht0+\ht2+\dp2\relax}%
  \bandleaf{\box0}{\box2}}

% Place a display block a fixed way down the leaf. NOT \vfil: the preamble sets
% \raggedbottom, whose own bottom glue competes with any \vfil pair and lands the
% block about a third of the way down by accident. A title page sits where it is
% put, so put it.
\newcommand{\dropto}[1]{\vspace*{#1\textheight}}

% A leaf composed as one box of exactly the text height, so \vfill inside it
% divides the leaf instead of competing with \raggedbottom's bottom glue.
\newcommand{\fullleaf}[1]{\thispagestyle{empty}%

% A display leaf: the 1853's own title and half-title pages, which are not running

    \renewcommand{\parasep}{\par\vspace{2.4\baselineskip}}%

\enleafn{2}{\input{fragments/en002}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Luke xviii. 1 — \emph{men ought always to pray, and not to faint} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,1 Thess. v. 17 — \emph{pray without ceasing} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Dan. vi. 10 — Daniel kneeling three times a day, as he did aforetime \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. cxix. 164 — \emph{seven times a day do I praise thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Gen. xxiv. 63 — Isaac going out to meditate at the eventide \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. cxix. 62 — \emph{at midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ex. xx. 24 — \emph{in all places where I record my name I will come unto thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. cxi. 1 — \emph{in the assembly of the upright, and in the congregation}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iv}\,The canonical hours, built out of Scripture rather than out of a breviary. \emph{Seven times a day do I praise thee} sets the number, and each of the seven is then given a text that shows somebody praying at that hour: Mark's \emph{a great while before day}, the psalmist's morning watches, the third hour at Pentecost, Peter's sixth hour on the housetop, the ninth hour at the Beautiful Gate, Isaac at eventide, the night watches — with midnight added from the same psalm that set the number. The office is being derived, not inherited, and that is the argument of the whole opening.}

\enleafn{14}{\input{fragments/en014}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{ii}\,Luke xxii. 41 — \emph{he kneeled down, and prayed} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Matt. xxvi. 39 — \emph{he fell on his face, and prayed} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. xliv. 25 — \emph{our belly cleaveth unto the earth} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ezra ix. 6 — \emph{I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to thee, my God} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Luke xviii. 13 — the publican smiting upon his breast \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Job iv. 14 — \emph{fear came upon me, and trembling} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Isa. lix. 11 — \emph{we roar all like bears, and mourn sore like doves} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Ps. cxxiii. 1 — \emph{unto thee lift I up mine eyes}; Ps. cxliii. 6 — \emph{I stretch forth my hands unto thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,1 Cor. ix. 27 — \emph{I keep under my body}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,The body's part in prayer, itemised like the hours and the places. Kneeling, prostration, the face to the ground, the head bowed and the countenance cast down, the smitten breast, trembling, groaning, eyes and hands lifted, the body kept under — seven numbered postures, each with the text of somebody doing it, and each with the affection it belongs to set opposite in a column of its own: \emph{Humbling, Confusion, Indignation, Fear, Sorrow, Longing, Avenging}. Three consecutive openings apply one method to the \emph{when}, the \emph{where} and the \emph{how}, which is what makes this front matter a treatise and not a preface.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{v}\,The reference here is the 1853 editor's, in his brackets, and his contraction is ambiguous. He writes \textup{[\emph{Ez.} ix. 6.]}, which in this volume could stand for either Ezekiel or Ezra — the two are elsewhere kept apart as \textup{\emph{Ezech.}} and \textup{\emph{Ezr.}} The verse is Ezra's: \emph{I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to thee, my God}, which is a countenance cast down and a confusion, exactly the posture and the affection the line names; Ezekiel ix. 6 is the order to slay at the sanctuary and has nothing to do with either. The volume settles it from inside itself — printed 171 prints the same verse in full as \textup{\emph{Ezr.} ix. 6, 7}, in the same penitential sense. Brightman reaches the same reading independently, tagging the sentence \emph{Of Ezra}.}

\enleafn{22}{\input{fragments/en022}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. xc. 13 — \emph{let it repent thee concerning thy servants} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Amos v. 8 — \emph{that turneth the shadow of death into the morning} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. civ. 30 — \emph{thou renewest the face of the earth} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. xiii. 3 — \emph{lest I sleep the sleep of death} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. xci. 6 — the Vulgate's \emph{business that walketh in darkness}, where the BCP has \emph{pestilence} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. lxv. 8 — \emph{thou makest the outgoings of the morning and evening to rejoice} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. iii. 5 — \emph{I laid me down and slept; I awaked} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Jer. xxxi. 26 — \emph{my sleep was sweet unto me} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Isa. xliv. 22 — God to Jacob: \emph{I have blotted out thy transgressions as a cloud} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,1 Thess. v. 5 — \emph{ye are all the children of light, and the children of the day}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ix}\,A promise about what God has done, asked back as a petition for what He has not yet done. Isaiah's verse is spoken by God in the perfect — \emph{Delevi ut nubem iniquitates tuas, et quasi nebulam peccata tua}, I have blotted out thy transgressions — and the prayer answers \emph{Dele … et dissipa}, blot thou out, scatter, with the possessive turned from \emph{thy} to \emph{mine}. The tense and the person are both reversed, and nothing on the page marks the change. It is the same move as at printed 321, where \emph{let it not return unto me void} — said by God of the word that goes out of His own mouth — is asked of the prayer going up from a man's; twice in the volume a guarantee is borrowed rather than argued from.}

\enleafn{24}{\input{fragments/en024}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Rom. xiii. 13 — \emph{let us walk honestly, as in the day} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xcv. 8 — \emph{harden not your heart}; Heb. iii. 13 — \emph{lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. xci. 6 — the Vulgate's \emph{noonday demon}, where the BCP has \emph{the sickness that destroyeth in the noon-day} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Matt. vi. 34 — \emph{sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. lxxviii. 33 — \emph{their years in trouble} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. xix. 2 — \emph{day unto day uttereth speech} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. cxliii. 8 — \emph{for I lift up my soul unto thee}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iii}\,Two lines here take the Vulgate against the Prayer Book, and the English follows the Vulgate. \emph{Negotium perambulans in tenebris} and \emph{dæmonium meridianum} — the business that walks in darkness and the noonday demon — are what Andrewes wrote; Coverdale has \emph{pestilence} and \emph{the sickness that destroyeth in the noon-day}. CONVENTIONS §9 makes the BCP our crib, and yields wherever he reaches past it, as he does here.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{v}\,This is the verse Part III mis-numbers, and here the volume gets it right. \emph{Anni mei in luctu} stands at printed 409 under \textup{Psal. xl. 9}, where the note has to say the reference is wrong; here the same half-verse is referred correctly to \textup{Ps. lxxviii. 33}. So the edition proves its own misprint across three hundred and eighty pages — and it confirms, from inside the book, a reading that was otherwise established only from Brightman. Both kept as printed.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{vii}\,Psalm cxliii does not stop here — it runs on across the next two openings, the plate marking \emph{Vers.} 9 and 10 below and \emph{Vers.} 11 on printed 27. One psalm carries the morning prayer over three leaves, and a reader who meets only the tagged verse 8 will take it for a single borrowed line.}

\enleafn{26}{\input{fragments/en026}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. cxix. 37 — \emph{turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Prov. iv. 25 — \emph{let thine eyelids look straight before thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Isa. l. 4, 5 — the Servant: \emph{he wakeneth morning by morning, he wakeneth mine ear} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. cxli. 8 — \emph{keep the door of my lips}, which is verse 3 \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Col. iv. 6 — \emph{let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Eph. iv. 29 — \emph{that it may minister grace unto the hearers} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,1 Sam. xxv. 31 — Abigail: \emph{no grief, nor offence of heart} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Neh. xiii. 22, 31 — Nehemiah's own refrain: \emph{remember me, O my God, and spare me} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Ps. xxxi. 6 — \emph{O LORD God of truth}; Prayer Book numbering \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Gen. xxxiii. 5 — Jacob to Esau: \emph{the children which God hath graciously given thy servant} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Ps. cxxi. 7 — \emph{the LORD shall preserve thee from all evil}\par}}

\enleafn{30}{\input{fragments/en030}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Luke i. 78 — Zacharias at the Benedictus: \emph{the dayspring from on high} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. i. 3 — the first word spoken over the creation: \emph{let there be light} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Rom. i. 19 — \emph{that which may be known of God is manifest in them} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Luke x. 26 — Christ to the lawyer: \emph{what is written in the law?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. cxviii. 27 — \emph{bind the sacrifice with cords, unto the horns of the altar} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Rom. vi. 4 — buried with him by baptism, to walk in newness of life\par}}

\enleafn{32}{\input{fragments/en032}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Heb. xiii. 20 — the epistle's closing blessing, on the God who brought again the great Shepherd \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ex. xxxiv. 6 — the LORD proclaiming his own Name to Moses in the cleft of the rock; Num. xiv. 18 — Moses pleading that same Name after the spies \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Rom. vii. 24 — \emph{O wretched man that I am} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Jon. ii. 8 — Jonah out of the fish's belly: \emph{they that observe lying vanities} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. cxli. 4 — the plate marks its reading as the Septuagint's \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Josh. vii. 19 — Joshua to Achan: \emph{give glory to the LORD, and make confession} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. xxxii. 5 — \emph{I acknowledged my sin unto thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Josh. vii. 20 — Achan's answer: \emph{indeed I have sinned} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Jer. viii. 6 — \emph{no man repented him, saying, What have I done?}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{vi}\,Both halves of the exchange at Ai, three lines apart. Joshua charges Achan to \emph{give glory to the LORD and make confession}; Achan answers \emph{thus and thus have I done}. Here the charge and the confession are alike the penitent's own words, with Ps. xxxii. 5 set between them — neither half meaning in the prayer what it meant in the history. The re-cutting is the composition.}

\originalsn{34}{\input{fragments/gr034}}{\input{fragments/la035}}{\textsuperscript{i}\,27 \textup{Τὰ ἔργα}] \textup{τὸ πλάσμα} \emph{apogr.} — \emph{cf. Lat.} \textup{Figmenta}, \emph{quod ex neutro fonte alio fluere potest}\\[1pt]\hphantom{x}27–28 \emph{punct. post} \textup{παριδῇς} \emph{del. apogr.} · \textup{ὁμοίωμα}] \textup{ὁμοίωμα.} \emph{apogr.}\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,27 \textup{Figmenta}] \emph{Vulg.} \textup{opera manuum tuarum}; \emph{ex Gr.} \textup{πλάσμα} \emph{pendet, non ex textu impresso}}{27}{1}
\clearpage
\markright{34}
\setnoted{1,6,7,9,13,16,20,23,27,29}
\enleafn{34}{\input{fragments/en034}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Job xxxiii. 27 — Elihu, on the man brought back from the pit \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Rom. ii. 1 — to the man who judges another and does the same; [Tit. iii. 11] — \emph{condemned of himself} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Hos. xiii. 9 — the LORD to Israel: \emph{thou hast destroyed thyself} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Dan. ix. 7 — Daniel in the exile, at the evening sacrifice \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Neh. ix. 33 — the Levites' confession, while the Law is read \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. xxxix. 7 — David, having first been dumb with silence \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. lxxxix. 46 — Ethan: how short a time God has made men for \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,1 Cor. vi. 20 — \emph{ye are bought with a price} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Ps. lxxxix. 47 — \emph{wherefore hast thou made all men in vain?}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,The Greek and the Latin part company in the first line. The Greek says \emph{thou hast chastened me for the things wherein I sinned}; the Latin gives \emph{Non recepi} and refers it to Job xxxiii. 27, \emph{it profited me not}. They are not renderings of one another. The English follows the Greek, per CONVENTIONS §6, and the Latin stands as the independent witness it is — see the note at 27 below.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{vi}\,A pun the English Bible cannot keep. Andrewes asks \emph{what is my expectation} and answers \emph{Substantia mea apud te est}, then four lines later \emph{Memorare quæ mea substantia}. Both are the Vulgate — Ps. xxxviii. 8 and lxxxviii. 48 — and both turn on substantia, which is why the two psalms can be set one on top of the other. The Authorised Version renders the first \emph{my hope is in thee} and the second \emph{remember how short my time is}, and the join disappears.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ix}\,\textup{Figmenta} is the evidence that this Latin column is a witness and not a shadow. The printed Greek reads \emph{the works of thy hands}, and the Vulgate of Ps. cxxxviii. 8 reads \emph{opera manuum tuarum}; the Latin here reads neither. \emph{Figmenta} — the thing moulded — can only render a Greek text that read \textup{τὸ πλάσμα}, which is what the manuscript reads and what the printed page does not.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{38}{\input{fragments/en038}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. li. 3 — \emph{my sin is ever before me} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Job vii. 11 — \emph{I will speak in the bitterness of my soul} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Isa. xxx. 15 — a promise refused: \emph{in returning and rest shall ye be saved… and ye would not} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,2 Cor. vii. 11 — the fruits of godly sorrow: \emph{yea, what indignation} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,1 Cor. ix. 27 — \emph{I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,1 Sam. xxv. 31 — Abigail to David: that this be \emph{no grief unto thee, nor offence of heart} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. xix. 12 — secret faults; and at 13 the Septuagint's \emph{strange sins} where the AV has \emph{presumptuous} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Matt. ix. 2 — to the man sick of the palsy: \emph{son, be of good cheer} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,2 Cor. xii. 9 — \emph{my grace is sufficient for thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Ps. xxxv. 3 — \emph{say unto my soul, I am thy salvation} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xii}\,Ps. xlii. 11 — \emph{why art thou disquieted within me?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xiii}\,Ps. cxvi. 7 — \emph{return unto thy rest, O my soul}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iii}\,The manuscript glosses this line in Hebrew, and the 1853 dropped it — the first of some thirteen places where it does so. \enleafn{40}{\input{fragments/en040}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. vi. 1 — \emph{rebuke me not in thine indignation} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xxxii. 6 — \emph{and so thou forgavest the wickedness of my sin}; Prayer Book numbering, and the Greek follows the Septuagint's \emph{ungodliness of my heart} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. xxxviii. 9 — \emph{my groaning is not hid from thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. li. 1 — \emph{blot out my transgressions} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. cii. 13 — \emph{the set time is come} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. cxxx. 30 — \emph{if thou shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?}, which is verse 3; the psalm has but eight \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. cxliii. 2 — \emph{in thy sight shall no man living be justified} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. cxix. 48 — \emph{thy commandments, which I have loved} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Isa. xxvi. 13 — \emph{other lords beside thee have had dominion over us} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Ps. lxxiii. 25 — \emph{whom have I in heaven but thee?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,John iv. 24 — \emph{in spirit and in truth}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{vi}\,The plate cites \textup{Psal. cxxx. 30}, and the psalm has eight verses. \enleafn{42}{\input{fragments/en042}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Heb. xiii. 7 — \emph{them which have the rule over you} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. iii. 15 — the first promise: the seed that bruises the serpent's head \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Deut. xxxii. 29 — \emph{O that they would consider their latter end} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Matt. xx. 6 — the labourers found standing idle in the market-place \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. xxvi. 4 — \emph{I have not sat with vain persons}; Tit. iii. 10 — a heretic, after the first and second admonition, rejected \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Job xxxi. 1 — \emph{I made a covenant with mine eyes} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Hos. ii. 6 — \emph{I will hedge up thy way with thorns}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}The Hebrew in the heading — \textup{\RL{סיג התורה}}, \emph{a fence about the Law} — is on the printed page, not supplied; one of the few places the 1853 let Andrewes' Hebrew stand. And the page ends by quoting the fence. The last resolution is Hosea's \emph{I will hedge up thy way with thorns}, so a rabbinic phrase for the Law's protective hedge opens the page and a prophet's hedge closes it. The twenty-odd resolutions between are what the fence is made of.}

\enleafn{48}{\input{fragments/en048}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Col. iii. 5 — \emph{mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Rom. vi. 4 — raised up to walk in newness of life \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Col. iii. 2 — \emph{set your affection on things above} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 Cor. xi. 31 — \emph{if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. lxv. 5 — \emph{the confidence of all the ends of the earth, and of them that are afar off upon the sea}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}This page sets the articles of the Creed against a discipline answering each — his death against mortifying the flesh, his burial against burying evil devices, and so down to the judgment. \sethead{The Second Day}
% ---------- opening 70 | 71 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{70}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Second Day}
\originals{70}{\input{fragments/gr070}}{\input{fragments/la071}}
\clearpage
\markright{70}
\setnoted{3,5,13,16,23}
\enleafn{70}{\input{fragments/en070}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. v. 3 — \emph{in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. i. 6 — the work of the second day: the firmament in the midst of the waters \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. cxlvii. 16 — \emph{he casteth forth his ice like morsels} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. cxxxv. 7 — \emph{he bringeth the wind out of his treasuries} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Lev. xxvi. 40 — \emph{if they shall confess their iniquity, and the iniquity of their fathers}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,This is the key to the whole of Part I. Each of the seven days opens from that day's work in Genesis, and prays out of it: the second day made the firmament, so the second day's prayer begins there and runs down through the waters above the heavens — showers, ice, dew, hail, snow, hoar-frost, winds — before it turns to confession. The days are not seven prayers that happen to fall in a week; they are the week itself, prayed through.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{78}{\input{fragments/en078}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,[Ps. xxxix. 8] — \emph{and my substance is with thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xxxi. 1 — \emph{let me never be put to confusion}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,The same half-verse is cited twice in this book under two different numbers. At printed 34 it is \emph{Substantia mea apud te est}, referred to \textup{Psal. xxxix. 7}; here it is the same clause referred to \textup{[Psal. xxxix. 8]}. The difference is the numbering, not the text: xxxix. 7 is the Authorised Version's figure and xxxix. 8 the Prayer Book's, which runs one ahead here. And the Prayer Book's figure is the one in square brackets — the 1853 editor's own mark for a reference he supplied. So the plate cites Andrewes' psalm on the AV's numbering and the editor cites it on the BCP's, on two pages of one book. Both stand as printed.}

\enleafn{82}{\input{fragments/en082}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Andrewes is praying for the places he himself served, under their etymologies. \emph{The Southern Spring} is Southwell and \emph{the Western Monastery} is Westminster, as the Latin column says outright (\emph{sc. Southwell}, \emph{sc. Westmonasterii}); with St Paul's between them these are his own prebends and his deanery. The English keeps the descriptive form because the Greek does, and the identification sits where Andrewes put it, on the facing page.}

\markright{84}
\setnoted{1}
\enleafn{84}{\input{fragments/en084}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,And these are his own three sees, in order. Chichester (1605), Ely (1609), and \emph{this present see} — Winchester, which the Latin glosses \emph{sc. Winton}. The phrase dates the prayer: he came to Winchester in 1619 and died in 1626, so this leaf of the Intercession was written, or last revised, in his last seven years. It is the one place in the book where the text says when it is.}
\clearpage

The likeliest mechanism is a dropped letter — \textup{xliii} for \textup{lxiii} — the same slip the volume makes at printed 411, where \textup{lxviii} stands for \textup{lxxviii}. Kept as printed.}

\setnoted{25}
\originalsn{96}{\input{fragments/gr096}}{\input{fragments/la097}}{\textsuperscript{i}\,25 \emph{voces Hebrææ Græcis respondentes in altero} στοίχῳ \emph{subjiciuntur apogr.}: \textup{\RL{יצר}} · \textup{\RL{שגגה}} · \textup{\RL{אשם}} · \textup{\RL{חטאה}} · \textup{\RL{פשע}} · \textup{\RL{עון}} · \textup{\RL{תועבה}}}{}{1}

\markright{96}
\setnoted{7,9,10,11,14,24,25,31}
\enleafn{96}{\input{fragments/en096}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,1 Kings viii. 47 — Solomon at the dedication, praying for those who repent in the land of their captivity \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xli. 4 — the verse of line 21 opposite, turned into the third person \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Luke xviii. 13 — the publican, standing afar off \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 Tim. i. 15 — Paul, \emph{of whom I am chief} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Luke xv. 18 — the prodigal: \emph{make me as one of thy hired servants} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. xxx. 9 — \emph{thou hast turned for me my mourning into dancing} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,2 Cor. vii. 11 — the seven marks of godly sorrow, which this column sets out\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{vii}\,Under these seven Greek words for sin the manuscript sets a Hebrew column, and the 1853 left it out. The apograph gives \textup{\RL{יצר}} · \textup{\RL{שגגה}} · \textup{\RL{אשם}} · \textup{\RL{חטאה}} · \textup{\RL{פשע}} · \textup{\RL{עון}} · \textup{\RL{תועבה}} — \emph{yetzer, shegagah, asham, ḥaṭṭa'ah, pesha, avon, to'evah}, the standard rabbinic vocabulary of sin, set as a lexicon beneath the Greek. It is not in the printed book at all. And the first of them is the word Andrewes glosses \textup{\RL{יצר טוב}}, the good inclination, at printed 76: so his \emph{φαντασία} is being read through the rabbinic doctrine of the two inclinations, which is a fact about his theology and not a footnote about his text. Recorded here; not restored to the page.}
\clearpage

\setnoted{2,11,12,13,15,17,19,24,26,27,28,29}
\enleafn{102}{\input{fragments/en102}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Rom. vii. 24 — \emph{O wretched man that I am} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,2 Sam. vii. 28 — David after the promise: \emph{thou art that God, and thy words be true} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Neh. ix. 31 — \emph{thou art a gracious and merciful God}, said of a people not consumed \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Rom. v. 20 — \emph{where sin abounded, grace did much more abound} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Tit. iii. 4 — \emph{the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,2 Cor. x. 1 — \emph{the meekness and gentleness of Christ} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Rom. ii. 4 — \emph{the riches of his goodness and forbearance and longsuffering} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Col. iii. 12 — \emph{put on therefore, as the elect of God, bowels of mercies} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Jas. v. 11 — \emph{the Lord is very pitiful, and of tender mercy} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Mic. vii. 18 — \emph{who is a God like unto thee, that passeth by the transgression of the remnant?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Acts xvii. 30 — \emph{the times of this ignorance God winked at} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xii}\,Isa. lvii. 11 — the Vulgate's \emph{I, keeping silence and as it were not seeing}, where the AV has \emph{held my peace}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,This is a catalogue of the Names of mercy, each with its proof-text, and the proof-texts are doing the work a lexicon would: \emph{bonitas} from Samuel, \emph{charitas} from Romans, \emph{hominum dilectio} from Titus — the Greek φιλανθρωπία — down to the \emph{viscera} of James. The page is closer to a concordance than to a prayer, and it is the ground the next page prays from.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{104}{\input{fragments/en104}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Neh. ix. 28 — \emph{many times didst thou deliver them} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Lam. iii. 33 — \emph{he doth not afflict willingly, nor grieve the children of men} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. lxxviii. 39 — \emph{he stirred not up all his wrath} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. ciii. 10 — \emph{he hath not dealt with us after our sins} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Hab. iii. 2 — \emph{in wrath remember mercy} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Joel ii. 13 — \emph{slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Isa. xl. 2 — \emph{she hath received of the LORD's hand double for all her sins}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,\textup{\emph{Thren.}} is Lamentations, the Vulgate titling the book \emph{Threni}, the Greek for the same thing — the dirges. It is the 1853's usual form and the band gives the English name, so the two differ on the opening by title only. The Latin here is the Vulgate's \emph{non enim humiliavit ex corde suo}, punishing not from the heart, which is a stronger thing than the AV's \emph{willingly} and is why the line reads \emph{not of thine own will}.}

\markright{110}
\setnoted{7,9,10,13,19,25,27,29}
\enleafn{110}{\input{fragments/en110}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,\textup{Vers. 24} — the plate's figure; the words printed on the line are verse 25 \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Rom. v. 2 — \emph{where sin abounded, grace did much more abound}, which is verse 20 \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Rom. ii. 4 — \emph{the goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,2 Tim. ii. 25 — \emph{if God peradventure will give them repentance} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,1 Pet. i. 19 — \emph{the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Acts iv. 12 — \emph{none other name under heaven} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. lxix. 5 — \emph{my sins are not hid from thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. xxxviii. 9 — \emph{my groaning is not hid from thee}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,The marks on this page are otherwise line-exact — \textup{Vers. 22} and \textup{Vers. 23} each sit on their own verse — which is what makes this one worth halting on. \emph{Infelix ego homo} and \emph{Quis me liberabit} are verse 24; \emph{Gratia Deo per Jesum Christum}, the line the figure is actually printed on, is verse 25. So either the figure is one short, or it is meant to cover the whole movement from the cry to the thanksgiving. Kept as printed, and neither reading is claimed.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The plate cites \textup{Rom. v. 2}, and the verse is Rom. v. 20. \emph{Superabundavit gratia} is the Vulgate of Romans v. 20 word for word; v. 2 is \emph{access by faith into this grace}, a different sentence. And the volume proves it against itself: printed 103 cites \textup{Rom. v. 20} correctly. A dropped nought, kept as printed — the fifth place in this edition where one page corrects another.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{vii}\,Two verses of the same shape, set one under the other. \emph{My sins are not hid from thee} and \emph{my groaning is not hid from thee} are different psalms — lxix and xxxviii — and Andrewes has put them together for the repeated clause, which is how most of this book is built. The English keeps both, unvaried, so the repetition reads as the design it is.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{114}{\input{fragments/en114}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Gal. iii. 10 — \emph{cursed is every one that continueth not in all things} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,1 Cor. xv. 56 — \emph{the sting of death is sin} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,1 Cor. xv. 20 — \emph{the firstfruits of them that slept} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,John xiv. 2 — the upper room, to troubled disciples: \emph{I go to prepare a place for you} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Heb. vii. 25 — \emph{he ever liveth to make intercession for them} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,John xiv. 3 — \emph{I will come again, and receive you unto myself} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Rom. ii. 6 — \emph{who will render to every man according to his deeds} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Luke xxiv. 49 — \emph{until ye be endued with power from on high}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,The Creed again, but each article answered by what it did. Not \emph{he was crucified} but the cross taking away the curse of the law; not \emph{he rose} but the firstfruits; not \emph{he sitteth} but the appearing and interceding. Compare printed 48, where the same articles are answered by a discipline the believer owes each of them. The Creed is recited three times in Part I and never twice to the same end.}

\sethead{The Fifth Day}
% ---------- opening 130 | 131 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{130}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Fifth Day}
\originals{130}{\input{fragments/gr130}}{\input{fragments/la131}}
\clearpage
\markright{130}
\setnoted{3,6,8,10,13,15,17}
\enleafn{130}{\input{fragments/en130}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. xc. 14 — \emph{O satisfy us early with thy mercy} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. i. 20 — the work of the fifth day: the moving creature that hath life \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. cxlviii. 10 — \emph{creeping things, and flying fowl} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Gen. i. 22 — \emph{be fruitful, and multiply} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. cviii. 5 — \emph{thy glory above all the earth} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,John xii. 32 — \emph{and I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all men unto me} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Col. iii. 2 — \emph{set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{vi}\,The verse is spoken of the Cross and is asked here of the Ascension. \emph{If I be lifted up from the earth, I will draw all men unto me} — and John adds, in the next verse, \emph{this he said, signifying what death he should die}, so the lifting up is the crucifixion. Andrewes hangs it under THE THINGS OF THE ASCENSION, immediately after \emph{be thou exalted, O God, above the heavens}, and takes the drawing to be the ascending Christ's. He does not argue the transfer, and the English does not smooth it: the same two words carry both liftings, which is presumably why he could put the one under the other.}
\clearpage
% ---------- opening 132 | 133 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{132}
\setnoted{}
\originals{132}{\input{fragments/gr132}}{\input{fragments/la133}}
\clearpage
\markright{132}
\setnoted{6,8,10,12}
\enleafn{132}{\input{fragments/en132}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ezek. xxxiii. 11 — the watchman's charge: \emph{why will ye die, O house of Israel?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Lam. v. 21 — \emph{turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ezek. xviii. 30 — \emph{so iniquity shall not be your ruin} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Dan. ix. 5 — Daniel's confession: \emph{even by departing from thy precepts}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iv}\,From here to the foot of the next leaf the page is Daniel's prayer, ix. 5–19, quoted straight through, and the plate marks every verse of it — \textup{[\emph{Vers.} 7.]} \textup{8.} \textup{16.} \textup{17.} \textup{18.} \textup{19.} They are not tagged one by one because the English lines are the verses; what the reader needs is to know he has entered a single prayer and not a catena. It is the great penitential prayer of the exile, made while Daniel was reading Jeremiah and counting the seventy years. And the volume comes back to it in Part II out of order — \textup{ix. 19} closes §22 at printed 339 and \textup{ix. 16} opens the intercession at printed 343, the later verse first. Part I prints the prayer whole and in sequence; Part II quarries it. Neither is conformed to the other.}
\clearpage
% ---------- opening 134 | 135 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{134}
\setnoted{}
\originals{134}{\input{fragments/gr134}}{\input{fragments/la135}}
\clearpage
\markright{134}
\setnoted{3,5,7,8,12,22,26,28}
\enleafn{134}{\input{fragments/en134}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Jas. iii. 2 — \emph{in many things we offend all} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Jas. ii. 13 — \emph{judgment without mercy to him that hath shewed no mercy} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,1 John i. 8 — \emph{if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,1 John ii. 1 — \emph{we have an advocate with the Father} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. lxxvii. 7 — \emph{will the Lord cast off for ever?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Heb. xii. 1 — \emph{the sin which doth so easily beset us} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Jas. i. 21 — \emph{superfluity of naughtiness}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iv}\,Lines 6–15 run 1 John i. 8 to ii. 2 continuously — the confession, the promise to the confessing, the Advocate, the propitiation — and the plate marks the verses as it goes. But the last clause is not quoted, it is ASKED. John writes that Christ is the propitiation for our sins, \emph{and not for ours only, but for the sins of the whole world}; the page turns the indicative into a petition — \emph{let him be} the propitiation for my sins, \emph{who is also for the whole world}. The world keeps the indicative and the man asks for himself. It is the method of printed 22 and 332 working inside a single sentence of Scripture.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{v}\,He doubles the preposition, and the doubling is the argument. \emph{Advocatum ad te apud te habeo} — an advocate to thee and with thee: the one pleaded before is the one pleaded to, and both are God. It is the court figure the book keeps returning to, and the English holds both prepositions rather than smoothing them into one.}
\clearpage
% ---------- opening 136 | 137 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{136}
\setnoted{}
\originals{136}{\input{fragments/gr136}}{\input{fragments/la137}}
\clearpage
\markright{136}
\setnoted{1,6,7,22,23,24,25,27,29}
\enleafn{136}{\input{fragments/en136}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,1 John ii. 16 — \emph{the pride of life} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Matt. v. 3 — \emph{blessed are the poor in spirit; for theirs is the kingdom of heaven} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Heb. xi. 6 — \emph{a rewarder of them that diligently seek him} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Job xix. 25 — \emph{I know that my redeemer liveth} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Matt. xvi. 16 — Peter at Cæsarea Philippi: \emph{thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,John iv. 42 — the Samaritans: \emph{this is indeed the Christ, the Saviour of the world} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,1 Tim. i. 15 — \emph{of whom I am chief} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Acts xv. 11 — Peter at the council: \emph{we shall be saved, even as they}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iii}\,The whole ladder is the Beatitudes, Matt. v. 3–12, and the plate marks every rung — but they are not tagged one by one, because the English lines ARE the Beatitudes and a tag would set the verse under the verse. What has been done to them is the point: they are turned from blessings into PETITIONS, and what is asked for is the CONDITION, not the promise. Christ says \emph{blessed are they that mourn}; the page asks to mourn, to hunger, to be persecuted — and the whole list is governed by \emph{Da mihi, Domine}, Give me, O Lord, standing under it at line 18. He asks to be given the poverty, not the kingdom.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{v}\,Three confessions in a row, and not one of them from the same quarter. Job's \emph{I know that my redeemer liveth} comes from outside Israel altogether; Peter's \emph{thou art the Christ} from the chief of the apostles; the Samaritans' \emph{this is indeed the Saviour of the world} from foreigners who had believed on the word of a woman. Andrewes sets them one under another without comment, and the arrangement says what no one of them says alone.}
\clearpage
% ---------- opening 138 | 139 ----------
\versoalign

\setnoted{2,4,6,10}
\enleafn{138}{\input{fragments/en138}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Job xix. 25 — the verse continuing: \emph{whom I shall see for myself} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xxvii. 15 — \emph{to see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. xxxiii. 20 — \emph{our soul waiteth for the LORD} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. xxxiii. 21 — \emph{let thy mercy be upon us, according as we hope in thee}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,\textup{Psal. xxvii. 15} is not an error: it is the Prayer Book's numbering. The Authorised Version has this verse at xxvii. 13; the BCP Psalter, which divides the psalm differently, has it at 15 — and the BCP is the book Andrewes had to hand, as printed 433 shows twice over. Do not "correct" it. The volume moves between the two numberings without warning, and only reading the verse tells you which is in use.}
\clearpage

\sethead{The Sixth Day}
% ---------- opening 148 | 149 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{148}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{The Sixth Day}
\originals{148}{\input{fragments/gr148}}{\input{fragments/la149}}
\clearpage
\markright{148}
\setnoted{3,6,9,12,13,14,16,17,18}
\enleafn{148}{\input{fragments/en148}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. lxxxviii. 13 — \emph{in the morning shall my prayer prevent thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. i. 25 — the work of the sixth day: the beast of the earth after his kind \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Gen. i. 26 — \emph{let us make man in our image} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. cxxxviii. 8 — the divine hand set to its own work \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Gen. ii. 7 — \emph{and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. viii. 6 — \emph{thou madest him to have dominion} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. xci. 11 — \emph{he shall give his angels charge over thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Gen. ii. 8 — \emph{and the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iv}\,Seven dignities in the making of man, counted out. A deliberation held beforehand, the divine hand set to the work, the breath of life, the image, dominion over the works, angels given charge, and a garden — each with its text. Andrewes is not retelling Genesis i but \emph{itemising} it, and the sixth day's prayer is built on the count: what man was made with is the ground of everything the page goes on to ask.}
\clearpage
% ---------- opening 150 | 151 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{150}
\setnoted{}

\setnoted{5,6,8,17,21,24}
\enleafn{150}{\input{fragments/en150}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,2 Pet. i. 4 — \emph{partakers of the divine nature} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. iii. 15 — the promise of the seed that should bruise the serpent \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Gal. iv. 4 — \emph{when the fulness of the time was come} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Hos. xiii. 16 — the prophet's word of a people fallen by its own iniquity \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Hos. xiv. 1 — \emph{so will we render the calves of our lips}, which is verse 2 \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Joel ii. 17 — \emph{give not thine heritage to reproach}\par}}
\clearpage
% ---------- opening 152 | 153 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{152}
\setnoted{8}
\originalsn{152}{\input{fragments/gr152}}{\input{fragments/la153}}{\textsuperscript{i}\,8 \emph{Græca om. apogr., quæ Hebraice leguntur}: \textup{\RL{ואתה תעל משחת חיי}} (\emph{Ion.} ii. 7), \emph{sub titulo} \textup{Τοῦ Ἰωνᾶ}}{}{1}
\clearpage
\markright{152}
\setnoted{1,3,8,12,20,25,26,30}
\enleafn{152}{\input{fragments/en152}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Amos vii. 5 — Amos staying the judgment: \emph{O Lord GOD, cease, I beseech thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Jonah ii. 8 — \emph{they that observe lying vanities forsake their own mercy} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Mic. vii. 18 — the closing doxology of Micah's prophecy \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Hab. iii. 2 — Habakkuk, after his complaint of God's silence has been answered \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Zech. iii. 3 — Joshua the high priest in filthy garments, and Satan at his right hand \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Zech. ix. 11 — \emph{by the blood of thy covenant} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. li. 2 — \emph{cleanse me from my sin}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iii}\,Here the manuscript reads HEBREW where the printed page reads Greek. The apograph gives \textup{\RL{ואתה תעל משחת חיי}} — Jonah ii. 7, \emph{thou hast brought up my life from corruption} — under its own heading, \emph{Of Jonah}; the 1853 set the Greek instead. This is the sharpest of the thirteen places where the printed book quietly drops Andrewes' third script, because here the Hebrew is not a gloss beside the text but the text itself. Recorded, not restored.}
\clearpage
% ---------- opening 154 | 155 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{154}
\setnoted{}
\originals{154}{\input{fragments/gr154}}{\input{fragments/la155}}
\clearpage
\markright{154}
\setnoted{2,5,9,13,15,17,18,23,24,25,28,29,31}
\enleafn{154}{\input{fragments/en154}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Zech. iii. 2 — \emph{is not this a brand plucked out of the fire?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Luke xxiii. 34 — \emph{Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Acts vii. 60 — Stephen, kneeling: \emph{lay not this sin to their charge} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Luke xxii. 44 — \emph{his sweat was as it were great drops of blood} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Matt. xxvii. 29 — \emph{a crown of thorns, and put it upon his head} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Heb. v. 7 — \emph{with strong crying and tears} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Matt. xxvii. 39 — \emph{they that passed by reviled him, wagging their heads} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. cxxix. 3 — \emph{the plowers plowed upon my back} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Ps. xxii. 17 — \emph{they pierced my hands and my feet}; Prayer Book numbering \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Matt. xxvii. 46 — \emph{Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani}, at the ninth hour \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,1 Cor. xi. 24 — \emph{this is my body, which is broken for you} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xii}\,Matt. xxvi. 28 — at the Supper: \emph{my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xiii}\,Ps. lxxxv. 2 — \emph{thou hast covered all their sin}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iv}\,The Passion assembled out of six books, and half of it proved from texts that are not narrating it. The thorns, the revilings, the strong cry, the neck under the cross and the pierced heart come from Matthew and John, who were telling the story; but the plowed back is the Psalter's \emph{the plowers plowed upon my back}, the pierced hands and feet are Psalm xxii, the covered sin is Psalm lxxxv, the strong crying and tears are an epistle's account of Christ's prayers, and the broken body an epistle about a supper. Half the members of the catalogue are proved from outside the Passion narratives, which is why the sequence reads as prayer and not as recital — the same method as printed 313, where the nailing is proved from after the resurrection, out of Thomas's mouth.}
\clearpage
% ---------- opening 156 | 157 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{156}
\setnoted{}
\originals{156}{\input{fragments/gr156}}{\input{fragments/la157}}
\clearpage
\markright{156}
\setnoted{3,20,24,28}
\enleafn{156}{\input{fragments/en156}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gal. v. 19 — the works of the flesh, which this column lists \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Gal. v. 22 — the fruit of the Spirit, which the facing column answers with \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Isa. xi. 2 — the gifts resting upon the rod out of the stem of Jesse\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,The psalm says \emph{turn US} and the plate says \emph{turn ME} — and changes nothing else in the line. Ps. lxxxv. 4 is \emph{Converte nos, Deus salutaris noster, et averte iram tuam a nobis}; the page sets \emph{Converte me, Deus salutaris noster, et averte iram tuam a nobis.} One pronoun is made singular and the two around it are left plural, so he puts himself alone under the verb of turning and leaves the congregation in possession of the mercy. Lines 1–10 are Ps. lxxxv. 3–7 quoted whole, every verse marked by the plate, so the verses are not tagged one by one. Third instance of the pronoun pattern — with printed 342's \emph{adauge mihi fidem} for the apostles' \emph{nobis}, and 343's \emph{in diebus nostris} for Hezekiah's \emph{meis} — and the only one where the change is partial inside a single line.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,Seven gifts here, and the Hebrew yields six. The column sets Wisdom, Understanding, Counsel, Might, Knowledge, Godliness and the Fear of the Lord. Isaiah's verse names \emph{the fear of the LORD} twice, and the Vulgate and the Septuagint render the first of the two as pietas, godliness — so the Latin Bible counts seven where the Authorised Version, translating from the Hebrew, counts six. The sevenfold gift the Church has always numbered is the Latin Bible's, and this page has it. The number is the Vulgate's, not a device of Andrewes', and it is the third register on this opening: works of the flesh, fruits of the Spirit, gifts of the Spirit, three lists that answer each other down the leaf.}
\clearpage
% ---------- opening 158 | 159 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{158}
\setnoted{}
\originals{158}{\input{fragments/gr158}}{\input{fragments/la159}}
\clearpage
\markright{158}
\setnoted{7,11,12,15,21,24,25}
\enleafn{158}{\input{fragments/en158}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,1 Cor. xii. 8 — the gifts of the Spirit, severally divided \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. cxxxviii. 8 — \emph{forsake not the works of thine own hands} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Gen. i. 26 — \emph{because} in thine image and likeness \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Rev. v. 9 — \emph{because} thou hast redeemed me by thy blood \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Tit. iii. 5 — \emph{because} of the washing of regeneration \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Rom. xi. 17 — \emph{because} thou hast graffed me into the good olive tree \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Eph. v. 30 — \emph{because} a member of his body\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iii}\,Five pleas, and every one of them begins \emph{Quia}. The prayer does not ask on the ground of need but on the ground of fact — because I am in thine image, because thou hast bought me, because thou hast washed me, because thou hast graffed me in, because I am a member. The repeated conjunction is the argument, and the English keeps it at the head of each line rather than varying it for elegance.}

\setnoted{2,3,4,5,6,7,10,11,12,13,14}
\enleafn{172}{\input{fragments/en172}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Matt. viii. 8 — the centurion: \emph{speak the word only, and my servant shall be healed} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Matt. viii. 25 — the disciples in the storm: \emph{Lord, save us} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Mark iv. 38 — \emph{carest thou not that we perish?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Matt. ix. 2 — to the man sick of the palsy: \emph{thy sins be forgiven thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Luke xvii. 13 — the ten lepers, standing afar off \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Mark x. 47 — blind Bartimæus by the wayside \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Mark vii. 34 — to the deaf man: \emph{Ephphatha, that is, Be opened} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,John v. 7 — the man at Bethesda, thirty-eight years sick: \emph{I have no man} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Luke xiii. 12 — to the bowed woman: \emph{thou art loosed from thine infirmity} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Ps. xxxv. 3 — \emph{say unto my soul, I am thy salvation} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,2 Cor. xii. 9 — \emph{my grace is sufficient for thee}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,The whole page is one request, asked ten times: \emph{say it to me}. Andrewes goes through the Gospels collecting the words Christ spoke to particular people — \emph{be opened} to the deaf man, \emph{thou art loosed} to the bowed woman, \emph{thy sins be forgiven thee} to the palsied, \emph{my grace is sufficient} to Paul — and asks for each of them in the first person. He is not recalling the miracles; he is asking to be the one they were said to. The Psalm and the Epistle at the foot are admitted on the same terms, as words spoken to somebody.}
\clearpage

\setnoted{3,20}
\enleafn{184}{\input{fragments/en184}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Rev. xix. 5 — \emph{praise our God, all ye his servants, both small and great} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Rev. xxi. 4 — \emph{for the former things are passed away}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,The manuscript has its largest silence immediately after this line. Andrewes' own book leaves three blank leaves here — six blank pages, more than it leaves anywhere else — and the next thing in it is the great personal intercession that the 1853 prints on the following leaf. The printed page runs straight on. What the blank leaves mean is not settled: they may mark the end of the seven days, or room left for matter never written. Nothing has been re-cut on the strength of them; the division is recorded here and in \textup{apparatus/CLASS-B-unit-boundaries.md}, which is where a decision about it would have to be argued.}
\clearpage

\setnoted{3,4,6,7,8,9,10,12,13,17,18,19,20,22,23}
\enleafn{204}{\input{fragments/en204}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Acts xii. 22 — Herod hailed as a god, and eaten of worms \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Acts xxiv. 27 — Felix, \emph{willing to shew the Jews a pleasure} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,2 Sam. vi. 16 — Michal despising David as he danced before the ark \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 Sam. ii. 13 — the fleshhook of Hophni, taking the priests' portion by force \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,2 Kings xi. 1 — Athaliah destroying all the seed royal \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Judg. xvii. 10 — Micah hiring a Levite at ten shekels a year to be his priest \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Acts viii. 18 — Simon offering money for the gift; Matt. xxvi. 16 — Judas, from the thirty pieces, seeking his opportunity \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,1 Tim. iii. 6 — \emph{not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Hos. iv. 4 — \emph{this people are as they that strive with the priest} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,2 Sam. xv. 31 — Ahithophel's counsel, prayed into foolishness \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Isa. xix. 11 — \emph{the princes of Zoan are fools}, Pharaoh's wise counsellors \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xii}\,Mic. vi. 16 — \emph{the statutes of Omri are kept, and all the works of the house of Ahab} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xiii}\,1 Kings xxi. 15 — the judges of Jezreel, and Naboth's vineyard \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xiv}\,Num. xxv. 5 — the plague at Baal-peor \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xv}\,Josh. vii. 26 — the valley of Achor, where Achan was stoned\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iii}\,This page names disasters by a single figure and expects the story to come with it. \emph{Hophni's fleshhook}, \emph{Michal's contempt}, \emph{Athaliah's plundering}, \emph{Ahithophel's counsel}, \emph{the judges of Jezreel}, \emph{the torrents of Belial}, \emph{the plague of Peor}, \emph{the valley of Achor} — each is one or two words standing for a whole history, and the deprecation works only if the reader supplies it. Nowhere else in the volume does so much depend on knowing what a name is for; without the notes below, the English of this page is a list of proper nouns.}
\clearpage

\markright{210}
\setnoted{4,7,8,9,10,11,12,13,16,18,20,22,27,30}
\enleafn{210}{\input{fragments/en210}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Heb. xii. 28 — \emph{let us serve God acceptably with reverence and godly fear} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,2 Cor. vi. 1 — \emph{that ye receive not the grace of God in vain} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Heb. xii. 15 — \emph{lest any man fail of the grace of God} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 Tim. iv. 14 — \emph{neglect not the gift that is in thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Gal. v. 4 — \emph{ye are fallen from grace} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,2 Tim. i. 6 — \emph{stir up the gift of God which is in thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,2 Pet. iii. 18 — \emph{grow in grace} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,\textup{[Act. xiii. 43]} — the 1853 editor's own bracketed reference: Paul and Barnabas \emph{persuaded them to continue in the grace of God}. It is the seventh and last rung of the ladder below, and the only one the plate did not print for itself. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,1 Thess. iii. 10 — \emph{might perfect that which is lacking in your faith} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Luke xvii. 5 — \emph{increase our faith}; Heb. iii. 6 — \emph{the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Isa. xlii. 3 — \emph{the smoking flax shall he not quench} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xii}\,Rom. v. 5 — \emph{the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xiii}\,Jas. iv. 6 — \emph{he giveth grace unto the humble} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xiv}\,Ps. lxxxvi. 11 — \emph{unite my heart to fear thy name}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,Seven verbs of grace in seven lines, and they make a single argument. Not to receive it in vain, not to fail of it, not to neglect it, not to fall from it — then to stir it up, to grow in it, to continue in it. Four negatives and three positives, each with its own epistle, mounting from the least a man can do to the most. The English keeps them as seven separate lines because the ladder is the point.}
\clearpage

\setnoted{13,18,20,22,24}
\enleafn{220}{\input{fragments/en220}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. lxxi. 9 — \emph{cast me not off in the time of old age} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Isa. xlvi. 4 — \emph{even to hoar hairs will I carry you} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Luke xxiv. 29 — the two at Emmaus: \emph{abide with us; for it is toward evening} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Jer. vi. 4 — \emph{woe unto us! for the day goeth away, for the shadows of the evening are stretched out} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,2 Cor. xii. 9 — \emph{my strength is made perfect in weakness}\par}}

\markright{222}

\markright{222}
\setnoted{18,19,21,27}
\enleafn{222}{\input{fragments/en222}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Eccl. xi. 8 — \emph{let him remember the days of darkness; for they shall be many} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Matt. xxii. 13 — \emph{bind him hand and foot, and cast him into outer darkness} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,John ix. 4 — \emph{the night cometh, when no man can work} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. cxxxiv. 2 — \emph{lift up your hands in the sanctuary, and bless the LORD}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iii}\,The verse the page is built on is only cited here, at the end. \emph{Venit nox, quando nemo potest operari} — and the leaf's first two words, standing unmarked at the head of the page, are \emph{Venit nox}. So the meditation opens by quoting John without saying so, runs the whole length of the page on the figure of the closing day, and only names the text where it turns the figure into a duty: to forestall the night by working some good thing. The reference at the foot is the plate's own, and it is the key to the leaf, printed twenty lines after the lock.}
\clearpage

\setnoted{2,4,8,12,15,19,20,22,23,25,27}
\enleafn{224}{\input{fragments/en224}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. xlii. 10 — \emph{my prayer unto the God of my life} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. lxiii. 5 — \emph{I will lift up my hands in thy Name}; Prayer Book numbering \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. cxli. 2 — \emph{the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Job xxxv. 10 — \emph{God my maker, who giveth songs in the night} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Isa. xxxviii. 12 — Hezekiah again: \emph{from day even to night wilt thou make an end of me} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ecclus. v. 5 — \emph{add not sin unto sin} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Prov. xxiv. 16 — \emph{a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Matt. xviii. 22 — \emph{until seventy times seven} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Jer. v. 30 — \emph{a wonderful and horrible thing is committed in the land} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Isa. xxx. 15 — \emph{in returning and rest shall ye be saved} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Deut. xxx. 2 — \emph{and shalt return unto the LORD thy God with all thine heart}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,\textup{Psal. xlii. 10} is the Prayer Book's figure, not a slip. The Authorised Version has \emph{my prayer unto the God of my life} at xlii. 8; the BCP Psalter numbers it 10. The same verse is cited the same way at printed 433, four hundred pages later — so the book is consistent in this, and it is further evidence that the Prayer Book Psalter was physically to hand. Do not correct it.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{vii}\,Two sevens, set against each other. \emph{A just man falleth seven times} is the measure of a day's failure; \emph{until seventy times seven} is the measure of the forgiveness asked for it. Andrewes puts them two lines apart and lets the arithmetic do the work — the second number is not merely larger, it is the first one multiplied, which is the point Christ was making to Peter.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{230}{\input{fragments/en230}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. xxxviii. 7 — \emph{my loins are filled with a loathsome disease} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xvi. 8 — \emph{my reins chasten me in the night-season}; Prayer Book numbering \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. ciii. 14 — \emph{he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. xvii. 8 — \emph{hide me under the shadow of thy wings} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. xxxii. 7 — \emph{in a time when thou mayest be found}; Prayer Book numbering \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. lxiii. 1 — \emph{early will I seek thee}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{vi}\,The psalm the volume mis-numbered at printed 92 stands here correctly as \textup{lxiii. 1} — the third page to give it right, after 106. \enleafn{234}{\input{fragments/en234}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. xxxi. 6 — \emph{O LORD God of truth}; Prayer Book numbering \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. xxxiii. 5 — Jacob to Esau: \emph{the children which God hath graciously given} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. cxxxix. 1 — \emph{thou knowest my down-sitting and mine up-rising}; Prayer Book numbering \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. cxxi. 8 — \emph{from this time forth, and even for evermore} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. lxiii. 6 — \emph{when I remember thee upon my bed} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. lxxvii. 6 — \emph{my spirit made diligent search} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. cxxxix. 18 — \emph{when I awake, I am still with thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. iv. 8 — \emph{thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{vi}\,\textup{Ad scopandum spiritum meum} — he keeps the spade. Ps. lxxvii. 6's \emph{my spirit made diligent search} is, in the Greek Andrewes used, a verb of digging over the ground; the evening examination is a turning of the soil, not a rummage. The same figure governs §41 in Part II, where the day's review is a recall of stragglers rather than a reveille. The English holds the spade in both places.}
\clearpage

\markright{238}
\setnoted{4,9,11,13,16,18,20}
\enleafn{238}{\input{fragments/en238}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Matt. viii. 8 — the centurion at Capernaum: \emph{Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof}. The prayer opens by taking a soldier's words about his house and applying them to a soul, which is why the roof of the next line is the roof of a house that is not a house. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,\textup{Vers. 20} — the plate's continuation reference, i.e. Matt. viii. 20, twelve verses on from the centurion: \emph{the Son of man hath not where to lay his head}. The complaint is Christ's own and it is turned round. He had nowhere to lay his head in the world; the prayer says there is no fit place to lay it \emph{here either}, in me. The same verse is made to indict the man praying, and the two references are joined for that purpose — which is only visible once you know that \textup{Vers.} means the book last named. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Luke ii. 7 — \emph{and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Matt. xxvi. 6 — \emph{in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Luke vii. 37 — \emph{a woman in the city, which was a sinner … brought an alabaster box of ointment} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,\textup{Vers. 38} — i.e. Luke vii. 38, the next verse: \emph{began to wash his feet with tears … and kissed his feet}. The plate cites the mouth's own act to justify the words \emph{impurum et execrandum os ejus}. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Luke xxiii. 43 — \emph{To day shalt thou be with me in paradise}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,The page is a legal brief made of precedents, and every one of them is a place Christ was received by the unfit. A cave and a manger, a leper's house, a sinful woman, her mouth, a thief on a cross — five occasions, five citations, and the conclusion drawn from them is \emph{Digneris ipse et me}, vouchsafe me also. He is not asking for an exception; he is arguing from a settled practice. It is the same method as §23's catena four hundred pages later, and the same as the ladder of unworthiness at printed 338, which is likewise built entirely out of approaches that succeeded.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The ground of the plea is Christ's own homelessness, turned round. The centurion's \emph{I am not worthy that thou shouldest come under my roof} stands above it; the reason given here is that the house is \emph{all desolate and fallen down}, and that \emph{thou hast with me no place worthy whereon to lay thy head} — which is the Son of man's own complaint twelve verses on in the same chapter, made a description of the soul he is being asked to come into. The plate marks it as a continuation of the centurion's verse, so the two are read as one passage.}
\clearpage

\versoalign
\markright{240}

\setnoted{15,21,22,23,24,26,27,28,29,30,31}
\enleafn{240}{\input{fragments/en240}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Rom. ix. 33 — \emph{whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Acts ii. 42 — \emph{they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Luke xxii. 19 — \emph{this do in remembrance of me} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 Cor. xi. 26 — \emph{ye do shew the Lord's death till he come} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,1 Cor. x. 16 — \emph{the communion of the body of Christ} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Matt. xxvi. 28 — \emph{shed for many for the remission of sins} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,1 Cor. v. 7 — \emph{Christ our passover is sacrificed for us} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Matt. xi. 28 — \emph{come unto me, and I will give you rest} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Col. ii. 14 — \emph{blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Heb. ix. 14 — \emph{purge your conscience from dead works} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,1 Pet. ii. 24 — \emph{by whose stripes ye were healed}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iii}\,Thirty-four names for one thing, each with its text. From here to the foot of the next leaf Andrewes sets out what the Sacrament \emph{is} — the token of the assembly, the memorial of the dispensation, the shewing of the death, the communion of body and blood, the remission of sins, an amulet against all that is unlucky, the quiet of conscience, the cancelling of debts — and gives every name a proof. It is a definition by accumulation: no one of the names is the definition, and the list does not resolve into a doctrine. That is why the page can be read by anyone who holds any of the doctrines, and why it was worth an entire meditation.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{242}{\input{fragments/en242}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. l. 5 — \emph{those that have made a covenant with me by sacrifice} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,John vi. 27 — \emph{the meat which endureth unto everlasting life} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,2 Cor. vii. 9 — \emph{ye sorrowed to repentance} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Luke xxiv. 31 — at Emmaus, \emph{their eyes were opened, and they knew him} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,John xiii. 15 — the washing of feet: \emph{I have given you an example} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,2 Cor. i. 22 — \emph{who hath also sealed us} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,John vi. 35 — \emph{I am the bread of life} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,John xiii. 35 — \emph{by this shall all men know that ye are my disciples} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,1 Pet. iv. 1 — \emph{arm yourselves likewise with the same mind} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,John vi. 56 — \emph{dwelleth in me, and I in him} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,1 Cor. xi. 31 — \emph{if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xii}\,Luke xxii. 20 — \emph{this cup is the new testament in my blood} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xiii}\,John xvii. 23 — \emph{that they may be made perfect in one}\par}}

\markright{250}
\setnoted{2,6,8,9}
\enleafn{250}{\input{fragments/en250}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Mark x. 17 — the rich young ruler: \emph{what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Acts ii. 37 — at Pentecost: \emph{men and brethren, what shall we do?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Acts xvi. 30 — the gaoler at Philippi: \emph{what must I do to be saved?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Luke iii. 10 — to the Baptist, three times over: \emph{what shall we do then?}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,Four askings of one question, and the answers differ every time. \emph{What shall I do?} is put by the rich young ruler, by the crowd at Pentecost, by the gaoler at Philippi, and three times over to the Baptist by the people, the publicans and the soldiers — and Scripture answers \emph{keep the commandments}, \emph{repent and be baptized}, \emph{believe on the Lord Jesus}, and a different practical charge to each trade. Andrewes sets them together without reconciling them.}
\clearpage

\enleafn{256}{\input{fragments/en256}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,2 Cor. vii. 11 — the revenge that godly sorrow works \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Luke xxiii. 34 — \emph{they know not what they do} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. lxxiii. 22 — \emph{so foolish was I, and ignorant} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,1 Tim. vi. 9 — \emph{foolish and hurtful lusts, which drown men in destruction} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Job xlii. 6 — \emph{wherefore I abhor myself} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. xliv. 15 — \emph{the shame of my face hath covered me}\par}}

\enleafn{258}{\input{fragments/en258}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Tit. iii. 11 — \emph{condemned of himself} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. cxliii. 2 — \emph{enter not into judgment with thy servant} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,1 Pet. v. 6 — \emph{humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Eph. iii. 14 — \emph{I bow my knees unto the Father} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Matt. xxvi. 39 — in the garden: \emph{let this cup pass from me} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. cxliii. 6 — \emph{I stretch forth my hands unto thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Luke xviii. 13 — the publican smote upon his breast; Jer. xxxi. 19 — Ephraim smote upon his thigh \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. cxxx. 1 — \emph{out of the depths have I cried} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Ps. xxxv. 10 — \emph{all my bones shall say, LORD, who is like unto thee?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Ps. ciii. 1 — \emph{all that is within me, bless his holy name}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{vii}\,Two men striking themselves, and Andrewes takes both. The publican in the Gospel \emph{smote upon his breast}; Ephraim in Jeremiah \emph{smote upon my thigh}. The brace on the page offers the reader either, and the two references stand side by side because neither gesture is the right one — the point is that repentance has a body, and Scripture shows it more than one way to move.}
