The figures are a hybrid, checkable twice on this page. \emph{Ps.} lxxxix. 16 — the AV divides that psalm so the verse is 15; the Vulgate, calling the psalm 88, has 16. \emph{Psal.} lvii. 12 — AV 11; Vulgate, calling it 56, has 12. The plate keeps the Vulgate's verse-figure under the Hebrew psalm-number, which is neither system entire — a fourth kind of numbering after the plain AV at 300, the plain Vulgate at 274 and the BCP at 433. An introduction claiming one Psalter is answerable for this page.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,\textup{et in sæcula, et in sæcula sæculorum} — not emphasis, not a doubled line. Ps. cxlv. 21 is Vulgate \emph{in sæculum et in sæculum sæculi}, for the Greek's \emph{unto the age, and unto the age of the age}. The English doubles because the Latin does; a later pass must not tidy one away.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,Here the plate is against both English Psalters and the English follows the plate. Ps. cxxxviii. 1 in the Hebrew has \emph{before the gods will I sing praise} — so the AV, and so Coverdale. The Latin is the Vulgate's \emph{in conspectu Angelorum}, the Septuagint's reading, and our English keeps angels. Not a departure from CONVENTIONS §9 but the case it exists for: the register is Coverdale's, the text is whatever Andrewes quoted.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,The one line not from the Psalter, and where the leaf turns. Rev. iv. 11 is the song of the four-and-twenty elders, arriving straight after he calls himself an unworthy sinner. Having exhausted the earth's book of praise he borrows heaven's — and the section ends in the twelve-membered doxology of Rev. v, so this is the hinge, not an interruption.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 345 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{345}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{345}{\input{fragments/la345}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{345}
\setnoted{2,3,8,10,12,22}
\enleafn{345}{\input{fragments/en345}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Luke ii. 14 — the angels over Bethlehem: \emph{on earth peace, good will toward men} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Rev. v. 12 — \emph{Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour}; Rev. v. 13 — \emph{be unto him that sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Matt. xxi. 9 — the crowds at the entry into Jerusalem: \emph{Hosanna in the highest}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,The plate cites two verses and sets twelve terms; neither verse has twelve. Rev. v. 12 gives seven — power, riches, wisdom, strength, honour, glory, blessing — and v. 13 four, all already among the seven. Five are therefore from elsewhere in the book: \emph{might} and \emph{thanksgiving} stand together at Rev. vii. 12, and \emph{salvation} in the cry at Rev. vii. 10, whose own words — \emph{unto our God which sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb} — are the two lines this grid runs into. The Apocalypse's own lists run to seven, twice; this one runs to twelve, and the page does not say why.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{v}\,The Confession of Praise opens by arguing that he has no right to make it — sinning and unrepentant, it would be \emph{more fitting} to lie prostrate and beg pardon than praise God with a polluted mouth. He praises anyway, on one ground: \emph{de ingenita Tua bonitate confidens}, trusting a goodness that is God's by nature and not a response to anything in him. The whole catalogue hangs from that clause.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{vi}\,The catalogue is the Roman law of persons. \emph{Liber} against \emph{Verna} is not free against slave but free against a slave born in the house; \emph{Legitimus} against \emph{Spurius} is the law of lawful issue; \emph{Homo civilis} against \emph{Barbarus}, citizen against outsider. He goes through the divisions of the \emph{status personarum} one by one, giving thanks for a legal condition as another man might for health. The same catalogue stands again at printed 428, in Part III §4's \emph{Quod} brace — with the antitheses stripped out (\emph{Vivo · Ratione præditus · Civilis · Liber · Ingenuus · Honesta stirpe}). Here every good is defined by what he might have been instead; there they are simply goods. \emph{Ingenuus} is the very term answering this page's \emph{non Verna}. Not to be conformed: the antitheses are the whole difference.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§24 \emph{Confessio Laudis}}
% ---------- printed 346 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{346}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§24 \emph{Confessio Laudis}}
\originalsone{346}{\input{fragments/la346}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{346}
\setnoted{1,6,12,16,23,26}
\enleafn{346}{\input{fragments/en346}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{v}\,1 Pet. i. 3 — \emph{begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ}; and in the editor's own bracket [4], \emph{an inheritance incorruptible, and undefiled, and that fadeth not away, reserved in heaven for you} — the page quotes both verses nearly entire. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Eph. i. 3 — \emph{blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,A proverb, not a description. \emph{Mali corvi malum ovum} — the Greek κακοῦ κόρακος κακὸν ᾠόν, \emph{a bad crow's bad egg}, said of a man whose badness is inherited and expected. The line thanks God not for respectable parents but for not being the sort of son people say that about.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,\textup{Non expositus} is the technical word for a child EXPOSED — carried out and left to die, lawful and ordinary in the world whose vocabulary this catalogue uses. It stands between \emph{educatus}, reared, and \emph{literatus}, taught. \textup{Mechanicus} here is a manual labourer, not a machinist; \textup{bardus} two lines above is dull-witted. The list thanks God for a place in a social order, in that order's own terms.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,The most concrete line in the catalogue names what poverty actually costs: an honest estate, \emph{so that I have need neither to flatter, nor to borrow.} Not wealth — enough not to have to fawn and not to have to owe. The two are set as one item.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,The gifts are divided as the schools divided them — \emph{bona gratiae, naturae, fortunae} — and only the first is subdivided, into redemption and calling. The same three stand again at printed 429 as \emph{Pro bonis \{ naturæ … \}}, the fourth recension parallel. Not to be conformed.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 347 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{347}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{347}{\input{fragments/la347}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{347}
\setnoted{3,8,9,14,22}
\enleafn{347}{\input{fragments/en347}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,2 Cor. i. 4 — \emph{who comforteth us in all our tribulation}; 2 Cor. i. 5 — \emph{as the sufferings of Christ abound in us, so our consolation also aboundeth}. Written out of the affliction in Asia in which he despaired of life, and quoted nearly whole above. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Dan. ii. 23 — Daniel's thanksgiving the night the king's dream was shewn him, with the executioner already appointed for the wise men of Babylon. His words stand in the four lines above; the bracket is the editor's.\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iii}\,Three pairs, and the columns are creation against redemption — what God made and marked (hands, countenance, name) against what Christ bought (blood, purchase, adoption), each left-hand title answered by the cost of the right. The two unpaired lines run the full measure and close the table Father, Son, Spirit, Church.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,\textup{Divisio} is the book explaining its own shape, and it is the most important page in Part II for anyone writing about this volume. What follows is not a prayer but an analysis of what a prayer contains; the leaf prints the parts, so they are not repeated here. Most of these words are actual section headings in this volume — \emph{Confessio peccatorum}, \emph{Confessio fidei}, \emph{Confessio laudis}, \emph{Deprecatio}, \emph{Intercessio}, \emph{Supplicatio}, \emph{Gratiarum actio}, \emph{Commendatio} — so the page is a table of contents for a book that never prints one. \emph{Compellatio}, \emph{Comprecatio} and \emph{Threni} appear here only.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{v}\,THE COLUMNS HERE ARE NOT A PAIRING — unlike the table four lines above, which \emph{is} read across. The \textup{Divisio} is one list broken into two columns, read down the left then down the right. The proof is the join: \textup{Deprecatio} stands at the foot of the left column and its members, \emph{of sin} and \emph{of punishment}, at the head of the right. Read across, it marries the address to sin.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 348 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{348}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{348}{\input{fragments/la348}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{348}
\setnoted{1,5,14,26}
\enleafn{348}{\input{fragments/en348}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{iv}\,Gen. xxxii. 10 — Jacob at the ford, before meeting Esau: \emph{I am not worthy of the least of all thy mercies, and of all the truth which thou hast shewed unto thy servant.} The volume has used this verse once already, at printed 338, where it stood first in a ladder of four sayings of unworthiness that were every one of them answered. Here it opens a confession instead. Never conform or cross-refer the two places.\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,The \textup{Divisio} continues, and here the columns ARE parallel — unlike 347's, which is one list wrapped. Left is the FORM of the prayer, right is what one prays THROUGH, headed by the bare preposition \textup{Per}. And the right column is the whole economy, in order and Trinitarian: Creation, Nurture, Governance, Preservation, Disposing; then Redemption opened into Conception, Nativity, Life, Passion and Death, Resurrection, Ascension; then, alone at the foot, Inspiration — the Son's part given eleven words to the Father's five and the Spirit's one.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The three little words between the columns are three different ways of joining a petition to God's acts. \emph{Quia} — because thou didst these things. \emph{Propter vel Per} — for the sake of, or through, them. \emph{Secundum} — according to them, as their measure. The same confession may be grounded on God's work as its cause, as its channel, or as its standard, and the page sets the three side by side without choosing. \emph{Et annunciabo} closes the list: the prayer ends by undertaking to tell.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,\textup{Ἄσκησις} is the one Greek word on the leaf, and it governs what follows: the \emph{exercise}, daily or nightly — penitence for evils, thankfulness for good things — and then a particular exercise, of age, of calling, of estate. The brace answers all three heads at once, and its worked example is a single man: \emph{si senex; in Clero; Episcopus} — an old man, in the clergy, a bishop. Andrewes was Bishop of Winchester and died in his seventy-first year. The one instance the scheme troubles to give is his own condition.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§25 \emph{Confessio Peccati et Protestatio Gratitudinis}}
% ---------- printed 349 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{349}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§25 \emph{Confessio Peccati et Protestatio Gratitudinis}}
\originalsone{349}{\input{fragments/la349}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{349}
\setnoted{1,4,7,8,10,12,16}
\enleafn{349}{\input{fragments/en349}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{ii}\,2 Sam. vii. 20 — David after Nathan brought him the promise of a house: \emph{what can David say more unto thee?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,2 Sam. ix. 8 — Mephibosheth, lame in both feet, Saul's grandson, called to eat at David's table continually: \emph{what is thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I am?} The bitterest self-naming in the Old Testament, and it is spoken by a man being shewn kindness. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,John xiii. 1 — the Supper: \emph{having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. cxvi. 12 — \emph{what shall I render unto the LORD for all his benefits toward me?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,1 Thess. iii. 9 — Paul of the Thessalonians: \emph{what thanks can we render to God again … for all the joy wherewith we joy for your sakes before our God?}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,Five questions in a row, and not one of them is answered. A section headed \emph{Protestation of Thankfulness} opens by finding nothing to say: David after the promise, Mephibosheth at the king's table, the psalmist, Paul. Each asks what can be said or given back, and the page simply sets the next question under the last. The third is not a question in its own text. John xiii. 1 is a statement — \emph{having loved his own, he loved them unto the end} — and the plate turns it into \emph{For that thou hast loved me hitherto?} The volume's habit of changing a verse's mood, elsewhere indicative into imperative, here makes an indicative interrogative.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{vii}\,From here the private prayer takes the shape of the EUCHARISTIC ANAPHORA. A \emph{spiritual sacrifice} is offered, received \emph{upon thy spiritual Altar}, and the Spirit is asked to be sent down in return — which is an epiclesis, the invocation that follows the offering in the Greek liturgies. And \emph{voluntary and involuntary} is their formula too, ἑκουσίων καὶ ἀκουσίων, which no English rite has. A man alone in his chamber is praying the shape of the Church's central action over himself.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 350 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{350}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{350}{\input{fragments/la350}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{350}
\setnoted{6,8,11,23}
\enleafn{350}{\input{fragments/en350}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Eph. iii. 20 — \emph{unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us}; Eph. iii. 21 — \emph{unto him be glory in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages, world without end} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. lxiii. 5 — \emph{my soul shall be satisfied as with marrow and fatness; and my mouth shall praise thee with joyful lips}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iii}\,The Lord's Prayer is not simply said here — it is TAKEN APART, in exactly the way the \textup{Divisio} two leaves back took prayer apart. The seven petitions are numbered, their verbs pulled out into a left column and their objects set right. And the brace is doing grammar: \textup{\{ Nomen / Regnum \} Tuum} sets one \emph{Tuum} to serve two petitions, which English cannot copy and must say twice. The prayer is being read as a structure, by a man who has just finished drawing the structure of prayer in general. The volume returns to it twice more — §26 \emph{Oratio Dominica variata} and §31's petition-by-petition meditation — and the three are not to be conformed; this is the plainest of them.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,The doxology is here, and the Latin Bible does not have it. \emph{Quia Tuum est regnum, potentia et gloria} is absent from the Vulgate at Matt. vi. 13 and from the Roman rite, which keeps it apart from the prayer; it stands in the Greek text and in the Greek liturgies. On a Latin page, its presence is a mark of which prayer-book was actually to hand.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§26 \emph{Oratio Dominica Variata}}
% ---------- printed 351 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{351}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§26 \emph{Oratio Dominica Variata}}
\originalsone{351}{\input{fragments/la351}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{351}
\setnoted{3,5,8,10,12,14,15,18,20,21,23,25,27}
\enleafn{351}{\input{fragments/en351}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{ii}\,Gen. xv. 1 — the word to Abram in the vision, before he had a son: \emph{I am thy shield, and thy exceeding great reward} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Num. xxiv. 13 — Balaam, the prophet hired to curse Israel: \emph{I cannot go beyond the commandment of the LORD, to do either good or bad of mine own mind.} The petition \emph{thy will be done} is put into the mouth of a man who wanted to do otherwise and could not. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Gen. xxviii. 20 — Jacob's vow at Bethel, with the stone still under his head: \emph{if God will give me bread to eat, and raiment to put on} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,1 Kings viii. 36 — Solomon at the dedication of the temple: \emph{forgive the sin of thy servants} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Matt. vi. 34 — \emph{take therefore no thought for the morrow} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. xl. 12 — \emph{innumerable evils have compassed me about} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. cxiii. 2 — \emph{blessed be the name of the LORD from this time forth and for evermore} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Job xxxiv. 30 — Elihu: \emph{that the hypocrite reign not, lest the people be ensnared} — set II's petition for the KINGDOM is a prayer against bad government. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,1 Sam. iii. 18 — Eli, when the child Samuel had told him the whole doom of his house: \emph{it is the LORD: let him do what seemeth him good.} Thy will be done, said by a man who has just been told he is ruined. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Job xxxi. 40 — Job's self-curse turned into the petition for daily bread by one word. Closing his oath of innocence Job says \emph{let thistles grow instead of wheat, and cockle instead of barley}; the plate sets \emph{pro tritico ne proveniat urtica, pro hordeo ne lolium} — let them NOT. The curse a man called down on himself if he lied becomes the fourth petition. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xii}\,Job vii. 20 — \emph{I have sinned; what shall I do unto thee, O thou preserver of men?} — Job's words made the petition for pardon \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xiii}\,Job xxxi. 1 — \emph{I made a covenant with mine eyes} — but the plate widens it twice: the covenant is made \emph{cum sensibus meis}, with all the senses, and its object is \emph{ut ne cogitem quidem de malo}, that he should not so much as think of evil, where Job's own concern was narrower.\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,The prayer said plainly on the leaf before is now said again SEVEN TIMES OVER, petition by petition, in other men's words — thy kingdom come by the word to Abram, thy will be done by Balaam, daily bread by Jacob's vow at Bethel, forgiveness by Solomon at the dedication. Then set II begins the seven again with different speakers. This is the method of §§33–34, the creed said in the words of ten confessors — applied here to the Lord's Prayer, and applied earlier. The petitions are never restated in Andrewes' own words at all.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 352 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{352}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{352}{\input{fragments/la352}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{352}
\setnoted{2,4,5,6,9,11,12,15,19,22,26}
\enleafn{352}{\input{fragments/en352}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Job v. 19 — Eliphaz: \emph{he shall deliver thee in six troubles: yea, in seven there shall no evil touch thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Exod. xxviii. 36 — the golden plate of the mitre, \emph{graven, like the engravings of a signet, HOLINESS TO THE LORD} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,1 Pet. ii. 9 — \emph{ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,John x. 9 — \emph{I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Matt. iv. 4 — the petition for daily bread said in the words that refuse bread. Christ to the tempter: \emph{man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.} This is the second time in two leaves that the fourth petition is made out of a text against bread — set II built it from Job's self-curse of thistles for wheat. The petition is never simply asked. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. xxv. 18 — \emph{look upon mine affliction and my pain; and forgive all my sins} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. xcv. 8 — \emph{harden not your heart, as in the provocation}; Heb. xii. 15 — \emph{lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you}. Two texts for the sixth petition, and both name a place in the wilderness where a people went wrong. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,2 Sam. xxiv. 16 — the angel stretching out his hand upon Jerusalem, and the LORD saying \emph{It is enough: stay now thine hand} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Ps. cxiii. 2 — \emph{blessed be the name of the LORD from this time forth and for evermore}. It opened set II on the leaf before and opens set IV here: the one verse the sets reuse is the one that blesses the Name, which is the petition they all begin from. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Ps. cxlii. 5 — \emph{thou art my refuge and my portion in the land of the living} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,Ps. cxliii. 10 — \emph{thy spirit is good; lead me into the land of righteousness}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,Set III opens the seven again, and its first petition is a thing engraved, not said. \emph{Sanctitas Domino} — HOLINESS TO THE LORD — is the inscription cut on the golden plate of the high priest's mitre, worn on the forehead. For \emph{hallowed be thy Name} the page does not quote a prayer but a piece of metal, and the two that follow keep the priestly setting: a royal priesthood, and going in and out by the door.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 353 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{353}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{353}{\input{fragments/la353}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{353}
\setnoted{2,5,7,11,12,15,17,21,25}
\enleafn{353}{\input{fragments/en353}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. cxlv. 15 — \emph{thou givest them their meat in due season}; Ps. cxlv. 16 — \emph{thou openest thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. li. 1 — \emph{have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. lxxxix. 23 — \emph{the enemy shall not exact upon him; nor the son of wickedness afflict him} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Prov. xviii. 10 — \emph{the name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Prov. viii. 15 — \emph{by me kings reign}; Prov. xxi. 1 — \emph{the king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will}. \textup{Flecte ad bonum} is in neither verse — the page adds the petition to the two texts. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Prov. xxx. 7 — Agur: \emph{two things have I required of thee; deny me them not before I die}; Prov. xxx. 8 — \emph{give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Prov. xx. 9 — \emph{who can say, I have made my heart clean?}; Ps. xli. 5 — the plate's figure, which is the Vulgate's verse-number under the Hebrew psalm-number: the AV and the Prayer Book have it at xli. 4, \emph{heal my soul; for I have sinned against thee}. Second page to show that hybrid, after printed 344.\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iv}\,Set V says the whole prayer out of the WISDOM books, almost all of it Proverbs — where sets I and II used men speaking in a story, this one uses a book of sentences. And its fourth petition is at last the natural one. After Job's self-curse at 351 and \emph{man shall not live by bread alone} at 352, set V reaches Agur's \emph{feed me with food convenient for me} — the one place in Scripture where a man asks for exactly daily bread. Three leaves, three treatments, and the plain sense comes last.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{vii}\,Prov. xix. 21 turned into the third petition, borrowing the Pater Noster's own verb. The proverb states a fact — \emph{there are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand} — and the page asks it: \emph{let there not be many devices in our hearts; but let thy counsel stand, et fiat}. \textup{Fiat} is the word of \emph{thy will be done}, imported into the proverb standing in for it.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 354 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{354}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{354}{\input{fragments/la354}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{354}
\setnoted{2,3,5,7,9,12,14,15,17,18,27,29}
\enleafn{354}{\input{fragments/en354}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{ii}\,Rom. ii. 24 — \emph{the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles through you} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Isa. lx. 12 — \emph{the nation and kingdom that will not serve thee shall perish; yea, those nations shall be utterly wasted} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Isa. xlvi. 10 — \emph{my counsel shall stand, and I will do all my pleasure} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Isa. lv. 10 — \emph{that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater}. \textup{Baculum panis}, the STAFF of bread, is not in that verse — it is the prophets' phrase for the staff that is broken in famine, brought in here to ask that it be given. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Isa. lxiv. 9 — \emph{be not wroth very sore, O LORD, neither remember iniquity for ever: behold, see, we beseech thee, we are all thy people.} The volume has used this verse once already, at printed 109, in the confession — here it is the fifth petition. Never conform the two places. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ezek. xiv. 4 — \emph{that putteth the stumblingblock of his iniquity before his face} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ezek. xv. 7 — \emph{I will set my face against them}, asked here as set not thy face against us \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,Luke v. 5 — Peter at the draught of fishes: \emph{Master, we have toiled all the night, and have taken nothing} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xi}\,2 Cor. iii. 14 — \emph{the vail untaken away in the reading of the old testament} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{xii}\,Ps. cxix. 12 — \emph{blessed art thou, O LORD: teach me thy statutes}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,The later sets are each quarried from ONE region of Scripture, and set VI completes the sweep — IV the Psalms, V Proverbs, VI the Prophets, where the first three ranged. The Lord's Prayer is said through the whole Bible, a region at a time. And set VI is the harshest: \emph{thy kingdom come} is asked as \emph{let all the nations and kings perish that serve not thy kingdom}. Nothing earlier is spoken in that voice, and the page does not soften it.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{x}\,A new section opens with a key, the plainest statement in the volume of how Andrewes reads a miracle. Five pairs read across: the world is the sea, men the fishes, the Church the boat, the preacher the fisherman, the Word the net. The draught of fishes set out as a working diagram for a man about to preach, hung on Peter's \emph{we have toiled all the night and taken nothing}. This table IS read across — unlike the \textup{Divisio} at 347.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§27 \emph{In Prædicatione}}
% ---------- printed 355 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{355}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§27 \emph{In Prædicatione · Ad Verbum · Ad Templi ingressum}}
\originalsone{355}{\input{fragments/la355}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{355}
\setnoted{2,3,4,8,17,18,19,28}
\enleafn{355}{\input{fragments/en355}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,1 Sam. x. 26 — of the band that went with Saul: \emph{whose hearts God had touched} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Eph. i. 8 — the plate's figure. The line wants verse 18, \emph{the eyes of your understanding being enlightened}, which is what \emph{illumina sensus cordis} renders; i. 8 is \emph{he hath abounded toward us in all wisdom and prudence}. Kept as printed — it stands on the volume's running list of wrong references with \textup{[Jer. l. 24.]} and \textup{[Dan. vi. 4.]} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. li. 15 — \emph{O Lord, open thou my lips}; Ps. lxxi. 8 — \emph{let my mouth be filled with thy praise}. Ps. li. 15 returns alone nine lines below — the one verse this page says twice, and the page is about nothing but the mouth. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Isa. l. 4 — \emph{the Lord GOD hath given me the tongue of the learned, that I should know how to speak a word in season}; Eph. iv. 29 — \emph{that it may minister grace unto the hearers} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Eph. vi. 19 — Paul asking prayer for himself: \emph{that utterance may be given unto me, that I may open my mouth boldly} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. lxxxi. 10 — \emph{open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. xxviii. 2 — \emph{when I lift up my hands toward thy holy oracle}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{iv}\,\textup{Carbo duplicis naturæ} — the COAL OF THE TWOFOLD NATURE — is a title for Christ, and it is not in Isaiah. The prophet's coal, taken from the altar with tongs and laid on his mouth, is read as the coal that is wood and fire at once, and so God and man at once; the tongs are what handles what cannot be touched. The reading is Greek — the ἄνθραξ of the Eastern liturgies, where the same coal is what the communicant receives — the fourth mark of that rite in six leaves, after 349's anaphora and \emph{voluntary and involuntary} and 350's doxology, and the strongest, because it carries a whole Christology in one noun.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. lxxxi. 10 is God's own command, answered as though it had been obeyed. \emph{Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it} — the psalm; \emph{Dilato os meum, Domine: Tu imple} — I have opened my mouth wide: do thou fill it. The condition is reported as performed and the promise called in. Not an indicative made imperative, but a promise TAKEN UP and its half discharged.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 356 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{356}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{356}{\input{fragments/la356}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{356}
\setnoted{1,10,12,17,20,21,23,26,27,29}
\enleafn{356}{\input{fragments/en356}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. xlviii. 9 — \emph{we have thought of thy lovingkindness, O God, in the midst of thy temple} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xxvi. 8 — \emph{LORD, I have loved the habitation of thy house, and the place where thine honour dwelleth} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Ps. xxvi. 7 — \emph{that I may publish with the voice of thanksgiving, and tell of all thy wondrous works} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. xxvii. 4 — \emph{one thing have I desired of the LORD, that will I seek after; that I may dwell in the house of the LORD all the days of my life} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Ps. xxvii. 8 — \emph{when thou saidst, Seek ye my face; my heart said unto thee, Thy face, LORD, will I seek} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. cxviii. 19 — \emph{open to me the gates of righteousness: I will go into them, and I will praise the LORD} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,John xx. 28 — Thomas, who would not believe till he had seen: \emph{my Lord and my God}. At the door of a building where nothing is to be seen, the worshipper says the words of the one apostle who insisted on seeing — and the next line is the blessing on those who do not. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,John xx. 29 — \emph{blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{x}\,Ps. xxxii. 6 — the plate's figure. \emph{I said, I will confess my sins unto the LORD} stands at verse 5 in the Authorised Version and at 6 in the Prayer Book Psalter, which is what the plate follows here — a third numbering system on show in this volume, beside the plain Vulgate and the hybrid at 344 and 353.\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{vii}\,The same verse is said twice on this leaf, once in each language — Ps. xxvi. 8 stands in Latin at the door, \emph{Domine, dilexi decorem domus Tuæ}, and returns fourteen lines later in Greek, Κύριε, ἠγάπησα εὐπρέπειαν οἴκου σου. The English renders both identically, which is the rule for a separated doublet; it is not a gloss and neither line may be dropped. He does not merely cite the Greek Psalter — he prays in it, which joins the coal at 355, the anaphora and the Greek formula at 349, and the doxology at 350.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§28 \emph{[Θωμᾶς}}
% ---------- printed 357 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{357}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§28 \emph{[Θωμᾶς — Pœnitetne?]}}
\originalsone{357}{\input{fragments/la357}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{357}
\setnoted{8,9,14,15,17,19,22,26,28}
\enleafn{357}{\input{fragments/en357}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{ii}\,Dan. vi. 4 — the plate's figure. Daniel kneeling three times a day is at vi. 10; vi. 4 is the presidents seeking occasion against him. Kept as printed — it stands on the volume's running list with \textup{[Jer. l. 24.]} and \textup{[Eph. i. 8.]} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Job xlii. 6 — \emph{wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. lxiii. 6 — the reference supplies a word, not a sense. \emph{When I remember thee upon my bed} is the psalmist doing well; the page takes only \emph{lectis} from it and makes the bed the thing to be avoided — if not on the ground and in ashes, yet at least not lying down. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Luke xvi. 19 — the rich man of the parable: \emph{clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Dan. i. 8 — Daniel at the king's table, who \emph{would not defile himself with the portion of the king's meat} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Lev. v. 16 — the trespass offering: \emph{he shall make amends … and shall add the fifth part thereto} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Deut. xxvi. 12 — the third year's tithe, \emph{the year of tithing}. The line offers a THIRTIETH part (\emph{tricesimam partem}), which is not what that verse commands, nor any tithe. Kept as printed and on the running list. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ix}\,2 Cor. viii. 3 — of the Macedonians: \emph{to their power, yea, and beyond their power, they were willing of themselves}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,Eleven pairs, and every one of them is a bargain struck downwards: \emph{if not … yet}. He sets a scriptural ceiling, concedes he cannot reach it, and names the least he will do instead — seven times a day like David, or at any rate three like Daniel; Solomon's long prayer, or at any rate the Publican's short one; Christ's whole night, or at any rate one hour. And the floor is repeatedly set by a BAD example, not a good one. If not on the ground in ashes, yet not in beds; if not in sackcloth, yet not in purple and fine linen — which is the rich man of the parable. Where the ceiling is a saint, the floor is a sinner: if I cannot be Job, let me at least not be Dives. The whole ladder ends by giving up on measure altogether — \emph{tamen quoad potentiam}, yet according to my power (2 Cor. viii. 3). The 21 references on this leaf are the densest in Part II outside the Passion, and the English lines name their own exemplars, so the band selects.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§29 \emph{Actus Adorationis}}
% ---------- printed 358 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{358}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§29 \emph{Actus Adorationis}}
\originalsone{358}{\input{fragments/la358}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{358}
\setnoted{2,6,10,12,15,17}
\enleafn{358}{\input{fragments/en358}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{ii}\,Rom. viii. 32 — \emph{he that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,1 John i. 7 — \emph{the blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Eph. iv. 8 — \emph{when he ascended up on high, he led captivity captive} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Matt. iii. 16 — \emph{the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Acts ii. 3 — \emph{there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,This is the LITANY's opening, in Latin, and it is a counterweight to the Greek marks of the last eight leaves. \emph{O God the Father, of heaven · O God the Son, Redeemer of the world · O God the Holy Ghost · O holy, blessed Trinity} — the Prayer Book's first four invocations, in the Prayer Book's order. And the English Litany's odd \emph{of heaven}, which is not idiomatic English, is a rendering of the very \emph{de cœlis} standing here: both this page and the Litany are drawing on the same Latin. The volume's liturgical debts run in two directions at once, and an introduction that argues only the Greek will be answerable for this leaf. One divergence, stated without conjecture: where the Litany's third invocation names the Spirit \emph{proceeding from the Father and the Son}, this one names him the Comforter.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 359 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{359}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{359}{\input{fragments/la359}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{359}
\setnoted{7,12,19,20,21,22,26,28}
\enleafn{359}{\input{fragments/en359}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Rom. xiv. 9 — \emph{to this end Christ both died, and rose, and revived, that he might be Lord both of the dead and living} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,Gen. xxiv. 7 — Abraham to his servant, before the journey for Rebekah: \emph{he shall send his angel before thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Matt. ii. 9 — \emph{the star, which they saw in the east, went before them} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Matt. xiv. 30 — Peter on the water: \emph{beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me}. The four examples are two and two: Abraham's servant and the Wise Men were GUIDED, Peter and Paul were RESCUED — one pair for the setting out, one for what may happen on the way. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Acts xxvii. 44 — the wreck off Malta: \emph{and so it came to pass, that they escaped all safe to land} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. lxviii. 1 — \emph{let God arise, let his enemies be scattered} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,Ps. cxix. 115 — \emph{I will keep the commandments of my God}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,A prayer for the dead, in a bishop of the Church of England's private manual, in the Requiem's own words. \emph{Defunctis requiem et lucem perpetuam} is the \emph{Requiem æternam dona eis, Domine, et lux perpetua luceat eis} of the Mass for the departed. The page has just laid the ground for it: Christ is \emph{Lord alike of the living and of the dead}, and the two halves of one company are named in turn — \emph{whose we are}, whom this world yet holds in the flesh, and \emph{whose also are they}, whom the world to come has already received unclothed of the body. The petition then divides its gifts along that line: to the living mercy and grace, to the departed rest and light. The English renders it plainly and does not soften it, which is the edition's rule and is the only honest course with a text of this kind.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§30 \emph{Oratio peregre profecturi}}
% ---------- printed 360 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{360}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§30 \emph{Oratio peregre profecturi · Septem Opera Misericordiæ}}
\originalsone{360}{\input{fragments/la360}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{360}
\setnoted{2,11}
\enleafn{360}{\input{fragments/en360}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The scripture foot is empty on this leaf because the leaf cites nothing, and that is correct. Both columns are the medieval MEMORY-VERSES, one verb to a work, made to be counted on the fingers — \emph{Visito, poto, cibo, redimo, tego, colligo, condo} for the corporal works, \emph{Consule, plecte, doce, solare, remitte, fer, ora} for the spiritual. They are not composed here; they are quoted, and every schoolman knew them by heart. The usual spiritual verse has \emph{castiga} where this sets \textup{plecte}, a harder word — to punish rather than to correct. Their presence says what kind of book this is: a working manual with a checklist in it, and it is another debt to the Latin West, beside the Litany on the leaf before.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,§31 is the volume's THIRD treatment of the Lord's Prayer, and the method is confession. §25 set it out plainly (printed 350) and §26 said it seven times over in other men's words (351–354); here each petition is stated, then admitted to have been failed, then asked. \emph{Holy art thou … to be held holy by all men, and by some more than by others, and by me first of all above many} — and then: \emph{Yet I have not so held it.} The petition becomes an indictment before it becomes a request. The three treatments are not to be conformed; this is the only one that turns the prayer against the man praying it.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§31 \emph{Πατὲρ ἡμῶν}}
% ---------- printed 361 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{361}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§31 \emph{Πατὲρ ἡμῶν} (the Lord's Prayer, petition by petition)}
\originalsone{361}{\input{fragments/la361}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{361}
\setnoted{7,11,14,15,18,19,21,25}
\enleafn{361}{\input{fragments/en361}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{iii}\,Matt. xviii. 24 — the servant brought in \emph{which owed him ten thousand talents} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Dan. ix. 8 — the plate's figure. The words are verse 7's: printed 35 sets the same pair at ix. 7, and printed 133 prints the two verses in order under their own \textup{Vers.} marks. Kept as printed. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Hos. xiii. 9 — \emph{O Israel, thou hast destroyed thyself}, which the Latin says in the first person \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. cxxx. 3 — \emph{if thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?} The same two lines stand verbatim at printed 41 under a figure reading cxxx. 30 — the closest witness the volume has against that misprint. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{viii}\,\textup{Vers. 7, 8} — i.e. Ps. cxxx. 7, \emph{with him is plenteous redemption}; Ps. cxxx. 8, \emph{he shall redeem Israel from all his iniquities} — asked here with the name of Israel gone\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,The third petition drives off two wills the plate never references — John i. 13's \emph{neque ex voluntate carnis, neque ex voluntate viri}. Then it turns the prayer's own geography onto the man saying it: \emph{fiat … de terra hac, quæ ego sum} — thy will be done upon this earth, which I am, the brace holding the clod twice, by this earth and upon it. That is §31's method entire: every clause is made particular before it is asked.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The fourth petition is asked twice here, and the second asking is the Eucharist: the temporal reading braced — \emph{health, peace, sufficiency} — then, on its own line, \emph{Da panem Angelorum ad salutem æternam}, the manna of Ps. lxxviii. 25, which the plate does not reference. The volume has never yet let this petition be simply asked (351, 352, 353); this is the fourth refusal and the only one that names what it wants instead.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,Four figures for four failures, and levelling them loses the descent: the huge sum of debt, \emph{prolapsiones fœdas}, \emph{recidivas crebras} (a physician's word for the sickness that returns), and \emph{volutabra diutina}, long wallowings — the \emph{volutabrum} is the swine's wallowing-place. From the counting-house to the sty.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{vi}\,The two verses travel together in this book and are here reversed, so that \emph{to thee righteousness, to me the shame} is now answered by \emph{my destruction is of myself}. And the Hosea stands in a third Latin form — \emph{mihi est ex me} (35), \emph{a me est} (the Evening prayers), \emph{mihi a me est} (here); none conformed to the others.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 362 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{362}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{362}{\input{fragments/la362}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{362}
\setnoted{2,3,9,12,21,26}
\enleafn{362}{\input{fragments/en362}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. lxxxvi. 13 — the psalm says \emph{thou HAST delivered}; the line asks \emph{Libera}, deliver thou — the indicative prayed back as a command \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{ii}\,Ps. xlii. 7 — \emph{deep calleth unto deep … thy billows are gone over me} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. ciii. 14 — \emph{he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust}, asked here as a petition\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,The verse is inverted: the psalm's cry of drowning gains a purpose-clause it lacks — \emph{Ut de abysso eripiat}, that it may pluck me out of the deep — so the second deep is God's mercy. Four lines on, the petition asks for the sins he cannot feel, and asks not pardon for them but light: \emph{ut possim confiteri}, that I may be able to confess.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,The sixth petition is re-said three times to get God out of the way of the tempting. \emph{Et ne inducas} — quoted headless, with no object at all — then \emph{ne me induci sinas}, suffer me not to be led in, then \emph{ne me sinas intrare}, suffer me not to enter. God leading, God permitting, and at last the man walking in himself — the middle being the ancient reading Cyprian and Augustine defended, the third going past both.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{v}\,Augustine, and famous: \emph{Hic ure, hic seca, ut in æternum parcas}, re-cast around the two ages as there spare, here burn, here cut.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{vi}\,The last petition descends out of theology into the man's own week and ends in the present tense. The evils are anatomised downward — flesh, Fiend, penal evils, the world to come, the world that now is — and then stop being categories: the malice of THIS sickness, \emph{wherewith I wrestle}, and the business I am entangled in. Both are present indicatives about the man holding the book — the same seam as the \emph{Divisio} at 347–348.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 363 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{363}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{363}{\input{fragments/la363}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{363}
\setnoted{4,5,13,24}
\enleafn{363}{\input{fragments/en363}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Dan. ix. 16 — Daniel in the exile: \emph{O Lord, according to all thy righteousness, let thine anger be turned away}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,This sentence stands three times in Part II in three Latin dresses, and the plate tags it once — here. Printed 343 (\emph{ut auferatur ira Tua}) and 373 (\emph{Ut avertatur a me justissima indignatio}) are unmarked. The Hosea two leaves back behaves the same way: a concordance built on the volume's own marks finds one of three and misses two.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The brace makes two superlatives commute, and both limbs are printed in both orders. \emph{Domino Reverendo, familiaque} is not resolved: "the Reverend Lord, and his household" may be his diocesan, his patron, or the master of a house he served in, and this witness cannot settle it.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,§32 begins here, and its heading is a technical word. Ἀνακεφαλαίωσις is the noun of Eph. i. 10's \emph{ἀνακεφαλαιώσασθαι}, to gather all things under one head in Christ — Irenæus' term, not a synonym for "summary." What it gathers is the Creed stripped to its events, Conception to Judgement, with no doctrine and no Church among them; and it closes not \emph{credo} but \emph{Fac me horum participem}, make me partaker of them.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,The \emph{Interpellatio Eucharistica} is the most doctrinally loaded line in Part II, and it is seven verbs long: \emph{Recolo, gratias ago, admoneo, recordor, commemoro, offero, vel peto ut offeras}. \emph{Admoneo} points the memorial at GOD — I put thee in mind — which is the patristic understanding of the anamnesis and not the ordinary Western one. And \emph{offero} is qualified in the same breath by \emph{vel peto ut offeras}: the sacrifice is offered, and then in one word the offerer is left an open question. A whole controversy hangs on \emph{vel}, and the English keeps it there and settles nothing. This leaf belongs with the anaphora at 349 in any account of what rite the book was written out of.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§32 \emph{Articulorum Fidei Ἀνακεφαλαίωσις}}
% ---------- printed 364 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{364}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§32 \emph{Articulorum Fidei Ἀνακεφαλαίωσις · Interpellatio Eucharistica}}
\originalsone{364}{\input{fragments/gr364}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{364}
\setnoted{1,6,7,11,15,18}
\enleafn{364}{\input{fragments/en364}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. xliv. 1 — \emph{our fathers have told us, what work thou didst in their days, in the times of old}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,The scripture band is nearly empty here because the plate cites almost nothing, and that is correct — §32 pleads the mysteries themselves, not texts about them, so what the leaf needs is its Greek opened. The two columns are not an antithesis — the Person on the left, the life on the right. \emph{Ἀπαρχὰς αἵματος}, the firstfruits of thy blood, is the Circumcision counted as the first shedding, eight days old; \emph{ἀπαρχή} is the firstfruits word of 1 Cor. xv. 20. The article is given a reason for standing in a plea about the Passion.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The left brace is Philippians ii turned into nouns and run BACKWARDS. \emph{Ἐκκένωσις} and \emph{ταπείνωσις} are the substantives of \emph{ἐκένωσεν} and \emph{ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτόν}, and after them come the enfleshing and \emph{σύλληψις ἐν γαστρί}, the conception in the womb: from the self-emptying down to the womb, later cause to earlier — the order of descent, not of narrative. \emph{Ἐκκένωσις} is rendered emptying-out, not "exinanition" — the κένωσις opened at printed 305.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,The Son of man with nowhere to lay his head returns here doing the opposite of what it did at printed 238. There it was turned round to indict the man praying — \emph{no fit place to lay it here either, in me}; here it is simply pleaded, one of Christ's own hardships beside hunger and thirst and watching. Not cross-referred and not to be conformed: this volume uses a text twice and never for the same thing.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,Two pleas are in the words of the events themselves, neither referenced by the plate: \emph{κατάληψιν ὡς λῃστοῦ}, apprehension as of a thief, Christ's own complaint in the garden, and \emph{συνοχὴ ἕως σταυροῦ}, the straitening of \emph{how am I straitened till it be accomplished}. Then three places under one preposition, garden, pavement and place of a skull, left untranslated as the plate has them.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{v}\,\emph{Ἐξομολόγησις} here is NOT confession of sin but the word's older sense, acknowledgement and so praise, which is why its limbs are \emph{of Grace, a Song} and \emph{of Praises, a Psalm}. A reader bringing the penitential sense across from §17 misreads the close of the section. The line above gives prayer an affirmative and a negative form, in Latin under Greek labels.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{vi}\,§33 opens here on one Latin line and then runs Greek to the end — twenty-one deliverances of the fathers, each a name and what he was delivered from. The argument is the psalm's own.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§33 \emph{Sicut patres, et nos libera, Domine}}
% ---------- printed 365 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{365}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§33 \emph{Sicut patres, et nos libera, Domine}}
\originalsone{365}{\input{fragments/gr365}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{365}
\setnoted{1,7,19,22}
\enleafn{365}{\input{fragments/en365}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{iv}\,Ps. xxi. 13 — the psalm's last verse: \emph{be thou exalted, LORD, in thine own strength: so will we sing and praise thy power}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,This is the \emph{Commendatio Animæ} — the deathbed prayer of the Western books — put into Greek. The Latin runs \emph{Libera, Domine, animam ejus, sicut liberasti Noe de diluvio · Abraham de Ur Chaldæorum · Isaac de hostia · Job de passionibus · tres pueros de camino ignis ardentis}, and it is among the oldest prayers the Church has, said over the dying. Andrewes keeps the form and changes three things: he turns it into Greek; he carries the roll on into the New Testament — the disciples in the storm, Peter in Herod's prison, Paul three times over; and he changes the petition from \emph{his soul} to us, \emph{καὶ ἡμᾶς ῥῦσαι}, so that a prayer for one man dying becomes a prayer the living say daily. The form is a Latin-West debt and the language is Greek, which is this book's whole difficulty on one leaf: it stands with the Litany at 358 and the memory-verses at 360 on one side, and with the anaphora at 349 on the other.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The preposition drops after David and the list runs on the bare genitive alone — \emph{ἀπὸ τοῦ Λαβάν} and \emph{ἀπὸ τοῦ Σαούλ}, then \emph{Ἠλίαν τῆς Ἰεζαβούλ}, \emph{Ἐζεκίαν τοῦ Ῥαψάκη}, and so to the end. The catalogue accelerates as it lengthens, and the English quickens with it. It is not a slip and is not restored.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,§34 opens on this page: \emph{Præparatio ad} Εὐλογίαν — a Latin heading with a Greek noun standing inside it — and under it \emph{Gratiarum Actio}. The blessing is prepared for by giving thanks first, which is the order of the whole section.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§34 \emph{Præparatio ad Εὐλογίαν}}
% ---------- printed 366 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{366}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§34 \emph{Præparatio ad Εὐλογίαν}}
\originalsone{366}{\input{fragments/la366}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{366}
\setnoted{2,4,6,16,18,25,26}
\enleafn{366}{\input{fragments/en366}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Ps. cxlv. 10 — \emph{all thy works shall praise thee; and thy saints shall bless thee} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,Rev. iv. 11 — \emph{thou art worthy to receive glory and honour and power} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. xxxi. 1 — \emph{in thee, O LORD, do I put my trust; let me never be ashamed}. Also the \emph{Te Deum}'s last line, and the Act of Hope opens on it. \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Ps. xxii. 9 — \emph{thou didst make me hope upon my mother's breasts}; Ps. lxxi. 5 — \emph{thou art my trust from my youth}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,This is the daily office's opening versicle, and it is quoted in its own form. \emph{Domine, labia mea aperies, et os meum annunciabit laudem Tuam} begins Matins in the breviary and Mattins in the Prayer Book. The line above it asks the same thing in the imperative, \emph{Aperi os meum}; the versicle then answers in the future indicative, \emph{aperies}, thou shalt open. The prayer asks, and the liturgy replies that it is already granted. Another debt to the Latin West.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,This sentence stands three times in Part II, and no two dresses agree. §24 opens with it at 345, §34 here, §41 at 384: \emph{Magis deceret} · \emph{Deceret magis} · \emph{magis deceret}, and \emph{confidens} · \emph{confisus} · \emph{confido}. Three sections begin by arguing he has no right to praise, and then praise. One word is not dress: 345, 374 and 384 read \emph{ingenita} — thine inborn goodness — where this leaf alone reads \emph{ingenti}, exceeding. The English follows the plate, and neither reading is claimed. 384 carries the office versicle too: §34 and §41 are near-twins, and are not conformed.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,The thanksgiving is built out of two liturgies. \emph{Gratias ago, adoro, laudo, benedico, glorifico} is the \emph{Gloria in excelsis} — \emph{laudamus te, benedicimus te, adoramus te, glorificamus te} — and the sentence that follows it, \emph{Dignus es, Domine Deus, accipere laudes et gratias}, is the Apocalypse's \emph{Thou art worthy}.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 367 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{367}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{367}{\input{fragments/la367}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{367}
\setnoted{3,6,14,17}
\enleafn{367}{\input{fragments/en367}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{i}\,Rom. v. 5 — \emph{hope maketh not ashamed}; Rom. viii. 24 — \emph{we are saved by hope}. The plate turns the reference across a line, \textup{[\emph{Rom.} v.} and \textup{5; viii. 24.]}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{ii}\,The Act of Hope is a word-catena, not an argument: thirteen texts in a row, and \emph{spes} or \emph{spero} stands in every one of them. They are not steps and do not build, and the English keeps \emph{hope} in every line. The band is nearly silent under them by rule — each line prints its own reference and gives its own substance (§3). \emph{Si occiderit me, sperabo} — the Vulgate's Job hopes, where the AV's \emph{yet will I trust in him} takes the other reading of a disputed Hebrew word.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,Four clauses, and not one of them finishes. \emph{Vellem, si plus} · \emph{Metuo, ne} · \emph{Doleo, quod non} · \emph{Gauderem, si}. Each breaks off exactly where its object would come, and the four are set two and two, wish against fear and grief against joy. The unfinished state is the point: nothing is supplied, and the reader finishes them himself.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,Under the Creed's own first word, \emph{Πιστεύω}, stand five sentences and not one of them is a credal article. They are five men's confessions, each labelled with whose it is — DAVID'S · PAUL'S · JOHN'S · PETER'S · NATHANAEL'S, and the plate prints each man's text under his name. With §32's Ἀνακεφαλαίωσις at 363 this is the second section running that puts something else where the Creed's propositions should be — there the bare events, here other men's sentences. The band is silent on these lines by rule — the plate names its own speakers (§3). The practice of captioning a text with whose it is, which this edition's tags follow, is the author's own; see his blessings at 425.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 368 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{368}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{368}{\input{fragments/gr368}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{368}
\setnoted{12,20}
\enleafn{368}{\input{fragments/en368}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The labels stop after Andrew, and what follows is doctrine with no speaker. Five confessions are captioned with whose they are — the Samaritans', Martha's, the Eunuch's, the Synod's, of the Apostles and Elders, Andrew's — and then three sentences stand unattributed. Two of them are the crux: \emph{justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law} is followed within four lines by \emph{by works is faith made perfect}, with the one Mediator standing between them. A Jacobean bishop set Galatians and James side by side at the end of a creed and added no connective, no ordering and no gloss; the English adds none either. And the roll has a shape: persons, then the Church assembled, then bare doctrine.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The Doxology is made of the two occasions when heaven and the crowd sang — the Nativity and the entry into Jerusalem — and all four evangelists' versions of the entry stand one after another, unconflated. Luke's crowd answers Luke's angels with the terms crossed: \emph{Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace} at the birth; \emph{Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest} at the gate. The inversion is Luke's own, and the page prints both so that it can be seen.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 369 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{369}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{369}{\input{fragments/gr369}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{369}
\setnoted{1,20}
\enleafn{369}{\input{fragments/en369}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The Sanctus opens the roll and is the one song here with no singer named; every other is captioned — the Angels' · all created things' · the Martyrs' · the four and twenty Elders' (ΤΩΝ ΚΔ΄, the number in Greek numerals) · the Marriage-song. The elders' \emph{which art, and wast} reverses the Sanctus' \emph{which was, and is} fifteen lines above, and the reversal is the Apocalypse's own — iv. 8 against xi. 17. Kept as printed; a corrector would level it.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The songs are taken in the Apocalypse's own order, from iv to xix, and the whole penitential sequence of Part II ends at the marriage supper: \emph{blessed are they which are called unto the supper of the Lamb}. A book that began in confession closes at a table — which is where §32's Eucharistic pleading at 363 was already looking.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§35 \emph{Oratio Tho. Bradwardini}}
% ---------- printed 370 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{370}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§35 \emph{Oratio Tho. Bradwardini}}
\originalsone{370}{\input{fragments/la370}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{370}
\setnoted{}
\enleafn{370}{\input{fragments/en370}}{}{This is the one borrowed prayer in Part II set out whole and under its author's name, with book, chapter and corollary given. The contrast is the point: at printed 362 the volume took Augustine's most famous sentence — \emph{hic ure, hic seca} — without a word of attribution, as it takes almost everything else. Here it stops, names a man, and gives a reference. Who he was, and the edition Andrewes is likely to have used, are in the list of sources at the back.\\[1pt]The prayer is built on one word, and an English that varies it destroys it. \emph{Teipsum} stands thirteen times on the page — \emph{Teipsum, Deus meus, Teipsum propter Teipsum … Teipsum desidero, Teipsum finaliter concupisco} — and again in each of the conditions, \emph{if thou give me not thyself}. Thyself, every time; never "thee", never "thine own self" for variety. And the lament is a chain in which every noun picks up the verb before it — \emph{amore languebo, languore mœrebo, mœrore dolebo, dolore lugebo et flebo}: love → languish, languor → mourn, mourning → grieve, grief → lament and weep. Four links, and they must be four in English. The three unanswerable questions that follow are each carried by a five-syllable adverb: \emph{inconsolabiliter · incessabiliter · interminabiliter}.\\[1pt]The prayer argues with God, and then tells him what would be unworthy of him. \emph{If thou render not thyself to me, thou renderest nothing; if thou give not thyself, thou givest nothing} — and, having hoped, \emph{thou dost not reward me, but tormentest me exceedingly}. Then the turn: \emph{Non est hoc Tuum}, this is not thy way, \emph{nullatenus congruit, nusquam decet} — it in no wise befits, nowhere is it seemly. The close answers the opening exactly, and in order: \emph{amem præ omnibus, quæram in omnibus, et tandem … inveniam ac teneam in æternum} — love, seek, find, hold.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§36 [\emph{Pro} intercession, headless]}
% ---------- printed 371 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{371}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§36 [\emph{Pro} intercession, headless] + \emph{De Pœnitentia}}
\originalsone{371}{\input{fragments/la371}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{371}
\setnoted{10,11,13,15,18,23,25}
\enleafn{371}{\input{fragments/en371}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{iii}\,Is. xxxviii. 15 — Hezekiah after his reprieve: \emph{I shall go softly all my years in the bitterness of my soul} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iv}\,Joel ii. 13 — \emph{rend your heart, and not your garments}; Ps. li. 17 — \emph{a broken and a contrite heart}, which the plate divides into two of the three \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{v}\,2 Cor. vii. 11 — the one Greek word on the page, Ἀγανάκτησις: the \emph{indignation} among the marks of godly sorrow, which is the sinner's anger at himself, and the same word §19 used of it \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vi}\,Ps. cxxx. 3 — \emph{if thou, LORD, shouldest mark iniquities, O Lord, who shall stand?} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{vii}\,Job ix. 3 — \emph{he cannot answer him one of a thousand}. The verse numeral is the 1853 editor's, supplied in his own brackets, and is kept in them.\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,§36 begins here with no heading at all, in the middle of an intercession — the page opens on a bare \emph{Pro}, and what stood above it is not in this book. And the list of the afflicted ends where no list of the afflicted ends: after the sick, the condemned, the widowed, the woman in travail and the man at sea comes \emph{præcipue non orantibus} — and chiefly for them that pray not. The last and greatest affliction is not praying, and it is the only one on the list that the sufferer cannot ask about himself.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,What follows is a SCHEMA, not a prayer — an outline of the parts of penitence with the text warranting each, like the \emph{Divisio} at 347. The band selects rather than tags every warrant: the lines are single words, and each prints its own reference. The English keeps the outline an outline and does not make sentences of it.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 372 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{372}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{372}{\input{fragments/la372}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{372}
\setnoted{7,8,13,19,20}
\enleafn{372}{\input{fragments/en372}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{v}\,Is. xxxviii. 15 — the plate's figure, and the same verse the leaf before drew \emph{bitterness of soul} from\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,Two technical terms stand in one brace and neither is a metaphor. The \emph{city of refuge} is Deuteronomy's, where the manslayer lives; \emph{secunda tabula} is the second plank after shipwreck — Jerome's \emph{secunda post naufragium tabula}, the standard scholastic name for penance as the remedy left to a man who has already been baptised. "A second chance" would destroy it, and so would translating the plank as an image rather than a term.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,God is made the suitor, and the page counts the ways. \emph{And God, for his part, sueth to us} — then six gerunds, each with its text and set two to a line: by proclaiming · by complaining · by swearing · by waiting · by promising · by threatening. The pairs read across, and they are not opposites but degrees: the proclamation answered by the complaint, the oath by the waiting, the promise by the threat. It is an argument that God has exhausted every means of persuasion.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,The two tables under it are the old catechism's, and they are meant to be read across. Prayer, fasting and almsgiving offer up the soul, the body and our goods; the same three overcome the devil, the flesh and the world, and are owed to God, to ourselves and to our neighbour. Three works, three faculties, three enemies, three debts — the medieval scheme of satisfaction, set down without a word of explanation because none was needed.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,Hezekiah said it of God; here it is said of the man praying, and said three times. The Vulgate's \emph{quid respondebit mihi, cum ipse fecerit} — what shall he answer me, seeing he hath done it — becomes \emph{cum ipse fecerim, fecerim, fecerim}: seeing I myself have done it, have done it, have done it. One letter changes the person, and the repetition is the confession. It is the volume's constant method at its sharpest — a text turned round on its speaker — and the English must strike the verb three times. Part III has the twin and it differs twice: \emph{cum ipse hæc fecerim} — once, not three times — and under a chapter figure one numeral short. Identical Latin gets identical English; the divergences stand and neither recension is conformed to the other.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§37 \emph{Confessio Peccatorum}}
% ---------- printed 373 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{373}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§37 \emph{Confessio Peccatorum}}
\originalsone{373}{\input{fragments/la373}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{373}
\setnoted{1,3,9,19}
\enleafn{373}{\input{fragments/en373}}{}{{\scriptsize \textsuperscript{ii}\,\textup{Ibid. et Vers. 17} — the plate's form, i.e. Is. xxxviii. 15 continued at verse 17: \emph{in my peace I had great bitterness} \textperiodcentered\ \textsuperscript{iii}\,\textup{Vers. 14} — \emph{like a crane or a swallow, so did I chatter: I did mourn as a dove}\par}\par\vspace{3pt}\textsuperscript{i}\,The whole leaf is one chapter of Isaiah, and it is quarried OUT OF ORDER — verse 15, then 17, then 16, then 17 again, then back to 14. Part I printed Daniel's prayer whole and in sequence; Part II mines Isaiah's, and the difference between the two habits is worth seeing. The opening line changes a word: Hezekiah goes softly all his years in the bitterness of his soul, and this goes over all his sins. Deliberate, and kept.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,He asks for what the verse four lines below already grants him. \emph{O utinam in amaritudine amarissima} — O that it were in bitterness most bitter — is a wish; and the verse then quoted says \emph{my bitterness was made most bitter}. The prayer petitions for the very thing the text it is quoting reports as done, which is this volume's method running the other way for once.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,Three penitents are named, and answered in a different order. He asks to be looked on with the eyes that looked on the Magdalen at the feast, Peter in the hall, the Thief on the cross — and then asks that with Peter he may weep, the Thief confess, the Magdalen love. The acts stay with their own people — it was Peter who wept, the Thief who confessed, the Magdalen who loved — but the sequence rotates by one, so that no name stands twice in the same place. It is not a slip and must not be tidied into parallel order. The movement closes on the reason: \emph{to whom much is forgiven, the same loveth much}, which the plate does not reference and which is the Magdalen's own verse.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 374 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{374}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{374}{\input{fragments/la374}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{374}
\setnoted{1,6,17}
\enleafn{374}{\input{fragments/en374}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The scripture band is empty from here to the end of §37 — printed 374 to 379 — because the plate cites nothing on any of them, and that is correct. It is not that there is nothing to cite. These two pages are made of unmarked allusion — Egypt's leeks, the prodigal's husks, Paul's \emph{who hath bewitched you}, Jacob at the ford — and after §36, where nearly every line printed its own reference, six unmarked leaves running are themselves worth noticing. The notes open what the plate leaves unmarked.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,Two bad bargains, and both are exchanges of a table for a trough. \emph{What, for leeks and for garlick, the Bread of Angels?} is Israel in the wilderness craving what it ate in Egypt, set against the manna; \emph{What, for the husks of swine, my Father's table?} is the prodigal. \emph{Panem Angelorum} is the phrase from printed 361, where the fourth petition asked for the Angels' bread instead of daily bread. There he asked for it; here he asks how he came to trade it away — the same words doing opposite work, which this volume does constantly and never marks. The two lines that follow turn other men's words on the speaker: \emph{who hath bewitched me} is Paul's rebuke of the Galatians, and \emph{then was it better with me than now} is Hosea's adulterous wife resolving to go back to her first husband. The prodigal, the Galatians and the wife all say \emph{I will return}.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,This sentence has stood before, at printed 366, and it is worth the comparison. There: \emph{whom I, a sinner, am not worthy to call upon, nor yet to name, nor to think upon in my heart}; here the same three verbs are braced and reordered — \emph{not worthy to name · nor to call upon · nor to think in my heart} — and the clause that answers them is the same in both, \emph{but for thy inborn goodness}. And that settles a question raised at 366. The volume reads \emph{ingenita}, inborn, at 345, here, and at 384; printed 366 alone reads \emph{ingenti}, exceeding. Three witnesses to one. Still kept as printed, and still nothing claimed — but the odds are now on the page.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 375 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{375}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{375}{\input{fragments/la375}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{375}
\setnoted{12,18}
\enleafn{375}{\input{fragments/en375}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,One word does duty twice, as adjective and then as imperative, and the English must let it. \emph{Mirifica est} — thy mercy is marvellous; \emph{Mirifica misericordiam Tuam erga me} — make it marvellous toward me. The psalm's \emph{shew thy marvellous lovingkindness} is behind both, and the page takes the description of what mercy is and asks for it as a thing to be done. It is the volume's commonest movement — the indicative prayed back as a command — turning here on a single word instead of a whole verse.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The boldest sentence in the section, and it is Jacob at the ford. \emph{Lord, if thou wilt that I depart from thee, give me another Thee; else will I not let thee go.} The last clause is Jacob's own — \emph{I will not let thee go, except thou bless me} — and the condition before it is impossible on purpose: there is no other Thee to be given, so the departure cannot be consented to. A refusal is being made to look like an obedience, and the English keeps the bargain intact and does not soften \emph{da mihi alium Te} into a wish.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 376 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{376}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{376}{\input{fragments/la376}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{376}
\setnoted{2,8,15}
\enleafn{376}{\input{fragments/en376}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The volume's own earlier page is the key to this unmarked one. \emph{Ariditas mea, ariditas mea! væ mihi!} is the shape of Isaiah's \emph{my leanness, my leanness, woe unto me}, with the book's own noun set into it — and printed 335 is where that noun was fastened to that verse, in a brace reading \emph{woe is me \{ for my dryness, [Is. xxiv. 16] / for my hardness of heart, / for the drought of my eyes, [Jer. ix. 1] \}}. Two of the three come back on this leaf with no reference at all — the dryness here, the \emph{fountain of tears} eight lines down. A concordance made from the plate's marks would join neither.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The doubling is the figure of the whole page: \emph{ariditas mea, ariditas mea} · \emph{exarui, exarui} · \emph{utinam … utinam vero et major} · \emph{væ mihi} twice. A man who cannot weep says everything twice. \emph{Exarui velut testa}, dried up like a potsherd, is the psalm's \emph{my strength is dried up like a potsherd}.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,A pun carries the surrender, and English has no single word for it. \emph{Extendam autem, quia intendere non possum magis} — he cannot strain the grief any tighter, so he will stretch it out instead, \emph{through all the years of my life}. Depth being impossible, he offers duration. The plea just above it is 2 Corinthians' — \emph{accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not} — the one measure in Scripture that asks nothing beyond a man's means, and the second time this volume has reached into that chapter for it.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 377 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{377}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{377}{\input{fragments/la377}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{377}
\setnoted{2,13,15}
\enleafn{377}{\input{fragments/en377}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The prayer argues God into consistency with his own commandment. \emph{This is the measure thou hast commended to us} — seventy times seven — \emph{to us, that we should render it among ourselves, and thou thyself not render the same?} Then the hinge: \emph{Absit enim ut plus in nobis perfectionis esse velis, quam in Teipso est} — God forbid thou shouldest will more perfection to be in us than is in thyself. The forgiveness Christ commanded of Peter is turned into a claim upon God, and the claim is that he cannot require of us a mercy he will not show. It is an argument, not a plea, and the English must not soften it into one.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,And the page does the arithmetic. Seventy times seven is left as a figure of speech everywhere else; here it is multiplied out — four hundred and ninety times over — and the mercy is trusted for the whole sum. A rhetorical number made a countable one, which is the same literalism that made the Lord's Prayer's \emph{earth} his own body at 361.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,The Publican is quoted and then bettered. \emph{Standing afar off} and \emph{smiting his breast} are Luke's; the escalation of the cry — \emph{to me a sinner · to me the most wretched sinner · to me the chief of sinners} — is not. And one parenthesis is the sharpest thing on the leaf: he smites \emph{that heart of mine} — which smiteth me not enough. The organ that ought to accuse him has to be struck from outside.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 378 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{378}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{378}{\input{fragments/la378}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{378}
\setnoted{14,16,26}
\enleafn{378}{\input{fragments/en378}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Romans vii. 18 stands here word for word and unmarked — \emph{velle mihi adjacet; perficere autem non invenio}, to will is present with me; but how to perform I find not. The same verb was already doing the work four leaves back at 375, where the grief \emph{lieth by me}, \emph{qui mihi adjacet}. Paul's word for the will that lies to hand seeds the whole movement, and the plate marks it in neither place.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,Two water-miracles are asked upon one heart, and the leaf ends on the first of them. \emph{Thou that turnest even the flint into standing water} is the psalm's rock struck in the wilderness — and twenty lines later, \emph{that I be not all flint}. The miracle is requested on himself. Between them stands \emph{Rorate, cœli, desuper}, the Advent introit, with its object changed: the heavens are not asked to rain down the Just One but to \emph{water the drought of my desert}. \emph{Ariditas}, the drought, is the word of 376 and the word printed 335 fastened to Isaiah — it threads three leaves and is marked on none of them.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,Four weepers, and they are not the four of two leaves back. David and Jeremiah, the Magdalen and Peter — where 373 asked for the eyes that saw \emph{the Magdalen, Peter and the Thief}. The Thief is gone, because the Thief did not weep; the company changes with what is being asked for.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 379 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{379}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{379}{\input{fragments/la379}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{379}
\setnoted{9,14,19}
\enleafn{379}{\input{fragments/en379}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The self-accusation is a piece of chemistry, and it does not work without it. \emph{Ah, pumex!} — pumice, the stone that will not hold water — and then \emph{vere calcem, in aqua frigida ferventem}: quicklime, which seethes when cold water is poured on it.
