The three lines that follow spell the point out: fervent where it least behoves, grieving enough where it behoves not, and cold, dry and dead where it behoves most. The image is of a substance that reacts violently to the wrong thing and not at all to the right one, and an English that makes \emph{calx} merely "lime" loses the heat.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,His tears having failed, he asks for a share in Christ's. \emph{Of the tears of thy Christ impart to me some, which in the days of his flesh he shed abundantly} — and then the ground: \emph{Supersunt in illo mihi, quæ in me mihi desunt} — there is left over in him for me what in myself is lacking to me. That is a treasury-of-merits sentence in a Church of England bishop's private book, applied not to satisfaction but to tears. Rendered plainly and unsoftened, which is the edition's rule; expect it to be noticed, as the prayer for the departed at 359 will be.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,§38 opens on the same page, and defines its terms: true penitence is a new life, and true confession is to repent without ceasing — \emph{keeping a perpetual sabbath}. The section that has just spent six leaves failing to weep ends by making penitence a manner of living rather than an act, and the new life is asked as the evidence of a new Spirit, not the cause of it.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§38 \emph{Oratiuncula post Confessionem}}
% ---------- printed 380 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{380}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§38 \emph{Oratiuncula post Confessionem} + \emph{Oratio Præparatoria}}
\originalsone{380}{\input{fragments/la380}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{380}
\setnoted{1,5,14}
\enleafn{380}{\input{fragments/en380}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The sentence begins on the leaf before, and its middle word is a term of art. \emph{Fomite} is the \emph{fomes peccati}, the tinder left in a man after baptism — the schools' name for what remains when the guilt is gone. Not a third word for temptation, which is what stands on either side of it: the sabbath is kept from the occasion that offers, the kindling that catches, and the danger that follows.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,He quotes the psalm, credits it to another man, and unsays it in the next line. The plate puts the attribution in the running text — \emph{(sic Psaltes, Psal. cviii. 1.)} — so that \emph{my heart is ready} is David's and \emph{I fear that mine is not} is his own. It is the volume's habitual movement inverted: everywhere else an indicative of God's is prayed back as a command and claimed; here an indicative of man's is quoted and declined. The three verbs following are the four-verb frame's third setting — \emph{metuo … cupio … doleo si minus} — after the empty frame at 367 and §37's filled one at 378.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,§39 opens at the foot of the page, the second attributed borrowing in Part II — where at 362 the volume took Augustine's \emph{hic ure, hic seca} with no credit at all. The doubt raised at transcription is settled: the passage reads so like Augustine that the tag looked composite, but Brightman, working independently from the sources, also gives Fulgentius of Ruspe. The counsel turns on a word English cannot hold — \emph{orator} is the man who prays and the man who speaks, so \emph{let him be an orator before he is a teacher} means let him be a pray-er first, and the clause before it puns again on \emph{oratio}. English chooses praying: the argument is about prayer, only the joke is about oratory.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§39 \emph{Ante Concionem Cautela cum Precatione ex Fulgentii l…}}
% ---------- printed 381 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{381}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§39 \emph{Ante Concionem Cautela cum Precatione ex Fulgentii l. i. ad Mon.}}
\originalsone{381}{\input{fragments/la381}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{381}
\setnoted{2,3,4,15}
\enleafn{381}{\input{fragments/en381}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The prayer changes its addressee in mid-passage. \emph{Veritas} is feminine, and the Latin slides from \emph{cleaving to the truth}, to \emph{of this very Truth I ask}, to \emph{Ipsam rogo} — Her I entreat. The section's longest petition is addressed to Truth, who is Christ; our English capitalises from the address onward, or a reader takes the close for a prayer to an abstraction.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,§40 begins here, and it is not a prayer. It is three catenæ of authorities — ἀφορμαί, handles for meditation — one set before each of three offices. The band is empty from here to 384 because every entry prints its own reference in its own line (§3a). The macaronic heading's word-order will not stay still: Greek first here, Latin first at 382 and 383. Kept as printed.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,The catena opens with the proof-text of the page above it. Fulgentius has just said \emph{let him be a pray-er before he is a teacher}; the first two entries are Martha's \emph{one thing is needful} and Acts vi. 4, \emph{we will give ourselves continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word} — prayer first and the word second, the order the Twelve chose when they had to choose. Nothing marks the join, and §39 and §40 sit on two halves of one page.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iv}\,The fathers enter by name and nothing more, where every scripture above carries chapter and verse — a saying was to be known by its author, not looked up. And the first three answer §37. After six leaves in which the penitent could not weep: \emph{if He prayed who was without sin, how much more ought a sinner to pray} · \emph{God is a hearer, not of the voice, but of the heart} · Augustine's \emph{more is wrought by groanings than by speeches}.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§40 Ἀφορμαὶ \emph{Meditationum}}
% ---------- printed 382 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{382}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§40 Ἀφορμαὶ \emph{Meditationum} (three catenæ: ante Preces Pœnitentiales · ante Intercessionum · ante Εὐχαριστίαν ἢ Εὐλογίαν)}
\originalsone{382}{\input{fragments/la382}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{382}
\setnoted{15,19,24}
\enleafn{382}{\input{fragments/en382}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,A Latin imperative governs a Greek infinitive, and the line is one sentence. \emph{Perge igitur} ἀγωνίζεσθαι ἐν προσευχαῖς — go on therefore to strive in prayers. The Greek is Colossians' own, where it is a participle describing somebody else: Epaphras, \emph{ἀγωνιζόμενος ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν ἐν ταῖς προσευχαῖς}, always striving for you in prayers. A report of what one man did is turned into the reader's own command — the volume's habitual movement, taken here on a participle rather than an indicative, as it was on the Baptist's ὁ αἴρων at 334. He did not think of himself as changing tongue mid-line, and the English keeps the sentence whole.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,A thanksgiving text opens the Intercessions, and Augustine's reading is the reason. \emph{Thanks be unto God for his unspeakable gift} is 2 Corinthians', and almost every reader will take the gift to be Christ. Augustine takes it to be the mutual intercession itself — the gift is that \emph{very many succour one another with mutual offices, and pray one for another, and give thanks.} Without that turn the first entry of the set has nothing to do with intercession at all, and the catena beneath it is built on the reading.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,The one place in Scripture where a failure to intercede is named a sin, and it stands at the centre of the set. Samuel, at the end of his rule, to the people who have asked for a king in his place: \emph{God forbid that I should sin before the Lord, in ceasing to pray for you.} The men he will not stop praying for are the men who have dismissed him. The verse comes in Greek, the Septuagint's, and only the hand that names it is Latin — \emph{inquit Samuel}.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 383 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{383}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{383}{\input{fragments/la383}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{383}
\setnoted{5,18,28}
\enleafn{383}{\input{fragments/en383}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Augustine refuses the devotional reading of Romans viii. 26, and the refusal answers six leaves of §37. \emph{Is thy spirit, or mine, unutterable — which is oftentimes no spirit at all, oftentimes cold?} The groaning that cannot be uttered is not the individual's. It is the whole Church's, pooled: \emph{because they all make up one Dove}, one besought fervently and another lukewarmly, \emph{hence come the unutterable groanings … out of the groanings of all in common.} After §37, where the penitent spent six leaves unable to weep, this is the consolation the book had been withholding — the intercession that counts was never his to produce.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The catena on praise opens by disqualifying the man who is to praise, and each entry after it takes something further away, until \emph{even the talkative are dumb} shuts both doors at once, speech and silence together. And the one beatitude among them is narrowed to fit: the Septuagint blesses the people that know the joyful sound, \emph{ὁ λαὸς ὁ γινώσκων ἀλαλαγμόν}; the plate drops \emph{ὁ λαός} and gives the plural, so the blessing falls on the single man who knows them. A catena for a private book, made private in the quoting.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,The section ends in Hebrew because no Latin or English Psalter will say what it needs. \RL{לך דומיה תהלה} — Psalm lxv. 2 in the Hebrew numbering — to thee silence is praise, with the 1853's own literal gloss set beside it, \emph{tacet tibi laus vel Psalmus}. The Vulgate takes the same consonants from another root and gives \emph{Te decet hymnus}, praise befitteth thee; the Prayer Book has \emph{Thou, O God, art praised in Sion.} Either would destroy the entry, which exists to say that praise falls silent — so the Hebrew stands and the English follows it. It is unpointed in the plate, without vowel or accent, and is the second Hebrew in Part II, after the Hosanna at 274.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 384 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{384}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{384}{\input{fragments/la384}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{384}
\setnoted{1,3,25}
\enleafn{384}{\input{fragments/en384}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The silence is given a mouth, and that closes the argument the leaf has been making. Andrewes glosses his own Hebrew gloss — \emph{it reacheth not thy works, it hath more of silence in it} — and then, out of the mouth of sucklings, with the psalm named. Praise fallen dumb is not a failure of praise but the infant's kind of it, and Psalm viii. 2 is the verse that has God perfecting praise out of exactly that mouth. A catena that opened by calling praise unseemly in a sinner's mouth ends by finding the one mouth that will serve.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The plate reads \emph{double} where the Septuagint reads \emph{tenfold}, and it is kept. Baruch's \emph{δεκαπλασιάσατε}, seek him ten times over, stands here as διπλασιάσατε, seek him double. The figure is not ornament: the verse is built on an exchange — \emph{as it was your mind to go astray … so, being turned} — and Andrewes' own line beneath does the same sum, \emph{as before we abounded in sins, so now … in good works.} Doubling keeps the two halves level; tenfold would not.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,Two trumpet-calls, and English has one word for both. ἐγκελευστικός is the charge, the call that sends men forward; ἀνακλητικός is the recall, by which the stragglers are fetched back. The evening exercise is the second of them — the mind roused in the morning is at evening \emph{called back … unto itself and unto its own captain}, which is what makes the set an evening one. The brace is the plate's own and is kept: two calls set against one occasion.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§41 \emph{Oratio præparatoria ante} Εὐλογίαν}
% ---------- printed 385 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{385}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§41 \emph{Oratio præparatoria ante} Εὐλογίαν + \emph{Monita et Meditationes præparatoriæ in Vespertina ad Deum elevatione mentis} (→ \emph{Scrutinium et Inquisitio, vel Examen})}
\originalsone{385}{\input{fragments/la385}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{385}
\setnoted{15,20}
\enleafn{385}{\input{fragments/en385}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,One verse is quoted twice over in two languages, and the English Bible has neither reading. The Greek is the Septuagint's Jeremiah — \emph{Βαθεῖα ἡ καρδία παρὰ πάντα}, the heart is deep beyond all things; the Latin line under it adds the Vulgate's \emph{tortuosum}, crooked. The Authorised Version has \emph{deceitful above all things}, which is a third thing again, and would put out both lights at once. The two readings are not a doublet but a stack, and the line beneath them needs both: \emph{the old man is covered over with a thousand wrappings} — wrappings answer the depth, and the thousand of them answer the crookedness. The English keeps the two lines distinct and conforms neither.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The brace is four levels deep, and its depth is its argument. \emph{What to-day thou hast} governs the day's four acts — done and said, read and written — and then four heads under which each is to be asked after: what beseems a man's calling, what confirms faith and obedience, what governs mind or body, what works salvation in himself or in others. Every one of the four acts is questioned under every one of the four heads, which is what the tall brace means and what any collapsing of it into a list would lose. Sixteen questions are being asked, not eight.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 386 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{386}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{386}{\input{fragments/la386}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{386}
\setnoted{12,28}
\enleafn{386}{\input{fragments/en386}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The evening examination is described in two borrowed vocabularies, and both are secular. First accountancy: Cato \emph{required of himself an account} of the day's business — \emph{rationem exigere}, a steward's audit — and he stands beside God reviewing each day's works, beside Pythagoras, and beside David, four precedents with no apology and no ranking. Then criminal law: \emph{in this Areopagite and nightly trial} — Athens' homicide court, which sat after dark, so the figure fits the hour as well as the business — \emph{shew thyself not the advocate of thy sins, but their judge}, at \emph{the bar of thine own mind}. And the sentence asked for is his own addition: Ecclesiasticus prays for scourges over the mind, and Andrewes adds that they spare not my sins.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,A whole Hebrew word is wrong in the plate, and it is wrong in a script the reader cannot check for himself, so the page shows both. The second word stands as \RL{חזתלת}, which is not a word; the sentence requires \RL{תוחלת}, \emph{hope}. The ground is Andrewes' own Latin on the facing page — \emph{Ecce spes fructus et salutis}, behold the hope of profit and of salvation — and the compositor's slip is legible as such: two sorts transposed and a zayin set for a vav, near-identical sorts in a line of upside-down work for a man with no Hebrew. It is the plate's and not the scan's: a second copy reads the same five letters. Kept exactly as printed, with the reading it requires set beside it and named as a reading.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 387 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{387}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{387}{\input{fragments/la387}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{387}
\setnoted{1,7}
\enleafn{387}{\input{fragments/en387}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,This is the sentence that settles the garbled Hebrew opposite, and it also sets the term of the exercise. \emph{Behold, the hope of fruit and of salvation shall be false to itself for ever} — Andrewes' own Latin for the rabbi's line, and its \emph{spes}, hope, is what the plate's Hebrew ought to read (386). Then the clause the whole \emph{Monita} has been driving at: \emph{unless thou rescue thy soul this very night}. And the discipline is given a dosage — \emph{some days, or one month at the least} — after which \emph{a perfect habit of virtue} is bred. An examination prescribed like a course of physic, with a term and an expected cure.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The voice changes here, and it is no longer Andrewes'. The paragraph is the 1853 editor's own note, printed at the seam and set in italic: the morning hymn follows \emph{out of the Alexandrine MS. of the King's Library} — the canticle-appendix of the Codex Alexandrinus — the evening hymn is added \emph{because it is old}, and Ussher's \emph{Book of the Creeds} is to be consulted on both. It is apparatus, not devotion, and is set as apparatus here; a reader who takes it for the book's own voice will think Andrewes is citing a seventeenth-century archbishop after his own death.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§42 ΥΜΝΟΣ ΕΩΘΙΝΟΣ / \emph{Hymnus Matutinus}}
% ---------- printed 388 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{388}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§42 ΥΜΝΟΣ ΕΩΘΙΝΟΣ / \emph{Hymnus Matutinus} + ΥΜΝΟΣ ΕΣΠΕΡΙΝΟΣ / \emph{Hymnus Vespertinus}}
\originalsone{388}{\input{fragments/gr388}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{388}
\setnoted{2,15,25}
\enleafn{388}{\input{fragments/en388}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The facing Latin is not a translation of this Greek: they are two recensions of one hymn, set side by side. The Greek is the \emph{Gloria in excelsis} as the Codex Alexandrinus carries it; the Latin opposite is the received Western Gloria, which is why it will not construe line for line. Our English follows the Greek, and the divergences stand where they fall: \emph{good will among men} is nominative, not the Vulgate's \emph{to men of good will}; and \emph{O Lord, heavenly King} has no \emph{God} in it, where the Latin and the Prayer Book both do. The Φῶς ἱλαρόν two leaves on is the opposite case, its Latin a close rendering of its Greek — only here are the columns two texts.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The Holy Ghost is named here, and the 1853 marks the fact in the other column with a row of asterisks. \emph{And O Holy Ghost} stands in the Greek among the persons addressed; the Western Gloria has no such clause, and the editor sets asterisks on the Latin leaf at exactly that line. Two leaves on the mark is reversed — the Latin has \emph{cum Sancto Spiritu} where the Alexandrine Greek does not, and the asterisks stand in the Greek column. The two rows fall on opposite sides of one question: where in this hymn the Spirit is named. They are apparatus, neither ornament nor a gap in the text, and both rows are kept.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,The footnote is the 1853 editor's, and its conjecture is offered as one. He thinks this \emph{may perhaps} be the very hymn Pliny described to Trajan — Christians meeting \emph{before daylight} on a set day to \emph{sing a Hymn to Christ as unto God, by turns among themselves}. The letter is Ep. x. 96, not the \emph{xxvii} printed here, almost certainly a misprint for \emph{xcvii}; kept as printed, with the volume's other uncorrected references.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 389 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{389}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{389}{\input{fragments/la389}}{}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 390 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{390}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{390}{\input{fragments/gr390}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{390}
\setnoted{5,7}
\enleafn{390}{\input{fragments/en390}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The Greek Gloria stops a clause short of the one the reader knows. It ends \emph{unto the glory of God the Father}, with no \emph{thou only art most high} — and the Latin opposite agrees with it, so here the extra clause is the Prayer Book's, not the Latin's. Nothing is supplied.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The relation between the two columns changes here, and a reader who has just crossed the Gloria must be told. The \emph{Φῶς ἱλαρόν} — O gladsome light, the oldest Christian hymn still in common use — is faced by a Latin that really is a rendering of it, tracking the Greek line for line and indent for indent. On the Gloria the columns were two recensions (388); here they are text and translation in the ordinary way, which is why no asterisks stand between them. One divergence from the received text is kept: \emph{ἄξιόν ἐστιν}, it is meet that thou be hymned, stands here as \emph{Ἄξιος εἶ}, worthy art thou — the second person, and the Latin's \emph{Dignus es} agrees, so it is the recension and not a slip.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 391 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{391}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{391}{\input{fragments/la391}}{}
\clearpage
\sethead{§43 ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΤΟΥ ΧΡΙΣΤΟΥ ΣΤΑΥΡΩΣΙΝ, Μονοστροφικά / \emph{In Chr…}}
% ---------- printed 392 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{392}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§43 ΕΙΣ ΤΗΝ ΤΟΥ ΧΡΙΣΤΟΥ ΣΤΑΥΡΩΣΙΝ, Μονοστροφικά / \emph{In Christum Crucifixum, Monostrophica}}
\originalsone{392}{\input{fragments/gr392}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{392}
\setnoted{12,15}
\enleafn{392}{\input{fragments/en392}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Twice on this leaf the facing Latin is the only guard against a plausible misreading of the Greek. \emph{Μακάρεσσι δαίμοσι} would give demons to anyone without the Latin's \emph{Beatisque Angelis} — in this Homeric register δαίμονες are the blessed spirits, and "demons" would be a serious and pious-looking error. The next line carries the graver case: the poem's most famous cry stands set as Πᾶς, Θεὸς ὢν, ἔθανες — \emph{πᾶς} cannot be construed at all, and the Latin's \emph{Qui, Deus immortalis, mortuus es?} gives the interrogative. Πῶς, \emph{how}: a wrong sort, kept as printed. Unlike the Hebrew at 386 this leaf survives in a single photograph, so there is no second copy to confirm it from.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,And three lines later the Latin must be refused. The Greek has the Father give the Son for a ransom \emph{ὑπ' ἐχθρῶν}, at the hands of enemies; the Latin opposite reads \emph{pro hostibus}, for enemies — the familiar theology of Romans v. 10. \emph{ὑπέρ} does not elide to \emph{ὑπ'}, so the Greek cannot be read as the Latin reads it. The English follows the Greek and leaves the crux standing, immediately after the same column twice rescued it.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 393 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{393}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{393}{\input{fragments/la393}}{}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 394 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{394}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{394}{\input{fragments/gr394}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{394}
\setnoted{14,16}
\enleafn{394}{\input{fragments/en394}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,A breathing is wrong here, and the sense turns on it. The line opens \emph{Ἡ οὐχ ὁράας} with a rough breathing, which makes it the feminine article and cannot stand before \emph{οὐχ}; what is wanted is \emph{Ἦ}, the interrogative particle. The Latin gives it plainly — \emph{Nonne cernis?}, dost thou not see? — and the English follows. Kept as printed: a compositor's mark, not the poet's.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,Two words are torn in half across a line-end, and the tearing is the poet's, not the printer's. \emph{ἀλ- / λ'} breaks here, in the middle of the blood; \emph{χέαν- / τ'} breaks thirteen lines on, in the middle of the pouring out. These are not the turned-line hyphens of a justified measure: the lines end far short of the measure, and the Latin opposite keeps the same lineation without splitting a word of its own. A word broken where the blood breaks — kept open, never closed up.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 395 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{395}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{395}{\input{fragments/la395}}{}
\clearpage
\parthead{Part III --- Confessio Fidei and after}
\sethead{§1 \emph{Confessio Fidei}}
% ---------- printed 398 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{398}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§1 \emph{Confessio Fidei}}
\originalsone{398}{\input{fragments/la398}}{epigraph}
\clearpage
\markright{398}
\setnoted{1,7,8}
\enleaf{398}{\input{fragments/en398}}{epigraph}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 399 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{399}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{399}{\input{fragments/la399}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{399}
\setnoted{2,4}
\enleafn{399}{\input{fragments/en399}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The Confession of Faith opens by confessing unbelief. \emph{I believe, Lord; help Thou mine unbelief} is the father of the epileptic boy's cry in Mark ix. 24, and it is set before the first article, as the door into the Creed. The Creed is not being recited but prayed, which is why every article below will be followed by what it is \emph{for}.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,Each article is numbered and then immediately told what it gives. \emph{In the Father, a natural affection · in the Almighty, a power that saveth · in the Creator, a Providence} — faith here is not assent to the articles but the thing each article yields, and the third yield is opened again into four: preserving, governing, perfecting, consummating. Creation is thereby made continuous with providence rather than an act finished in the past.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 400 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{400}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{400}{\input{fragments/la400}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{400}
\setnoted{4,5}
\enleafn{400}{\input{fragments/en400}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The lordship is given two grounds and the brace holds them equal — \emph{Our Lord}, because Creator and because Redeemer. Neither is subordinated to the other, and the brace is the plate's own.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,Every article of the Creed is given a purpose, and each purpose is exactly reciprocal to us. Conceived, to purge the uncleanness of our conception · born, to purge our nativity · \emph{suffered what we must have suffered, that we should not suffer it} · descended into hell, \emph{whither we must have gone, that we should never go down thither} · ascended, \emph{to prepare a place for us, where we had no right at all}. The pattern is not decoration but the section's method: each thing done is set against the thing it excused us, so the Creed is read as a ledger of exchanges. The English keeps the parallel clauses parallel, at whatever cost in elegance.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 401 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{401}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{401}{\input{fragments/la401}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{401}
\setnoted{8,23}
\enleafn{401}{\input{fragments/en401}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The Spirit's manner of working is stated in a pair of adverbs, and the pair is the doctrine. \emph{From without and invisibly, but effectually and manifestly in us working} — the source outside the man and hidden, the effect inside him and plain to see. The offices that follow are equally exact, and gifts are kept distinct from fruits: the one given, the other grown.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The preposition drops at the fourth article, and its dropping is the whole of the ancient distinction. The Latin has \emph{In Deum}, \emph{In Jesum Christum}, \emph{3. In Spiritum Sanctum} — and then \emph{4. Sanctam Catholicam Ecclesiam}, accusative, with no \emph{in}. We believe \emph{in} God; we believe the Church — a difference the Fathers made much of and this page makes without a word of comment. The Church is then defined by what the Spirit does: \emph{them whom the Spirit calleth out of the whole world}. The English keeps the preposition where the Latin has it and drops it where the Latin drops it.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 402 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{402}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{402}{\input{fragments/la402}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{402}
\setnoted{9,23}
\enleafn{402}{\input{fragments/en402}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The Creed begins again here, and this is the second of three passes over it. \emph{I believe, Lord; supply the defects of my faith} answers the opening \emph{help Thou mine unbelief} at 399 — and what follows is no longer what each article is, but what each Person is owed: the Father loved, the Almighty revered, the Creator trusted with a soul, the Son thanked. The articles have not changed; the verbs have.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The two conquests are kept apart, and each is given its own event. Conqueror over hell, in His Descent · conqueror over death, in His Resurrection — where a looser hand would have let one victory cover both. The series then runs on past the conquests into offices — \emph{Forerunner} in the Ascension, \emph{Advocate} in the Session, \emph{finisher of our faith} in the second Advent — so that every clause of the Creed is doing a distinct piece of work, and none is left as mere narrative.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 403 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{403}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{403}{\input{fragments/la403}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{403}
\setnoted{4,16}
\enleafn{403}{\input{fragments/en403}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,And here the Creed is run a THIRD time, now as a pattern to be reproduced. \emph{That Christ Himself may be formed in us} — after what the articles are (399–402) and what they are owed (402), what they must become in the believer: the Conception answered by faith, the Nativity by humility, the Passion by a fellow-feeling, the Descent into hell by frequent meditation going down into it, the Resurrection by newness of life, the Ascension by seeking the things above. Three passes over one Creed is the section's whole architecture, and a reader who takes the numbered clauses for a list will miss that the list has been begun over twice.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,Four verbs for one object, and the fourth completes the parallel. \emph{To avenge, to crucify, to mortify, to bury} the sin that is in us — the burial is what makes it conformity rather than mere severity: the sin is not only killed but put where Christ's body was put, and the next clause goes down into hell after it. The English keeps all four and lets none absorb another.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 404 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{404}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{404}{\input{fragments/la404}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{404}
\setnoted{3,28}
\enleafn{404}{\input{fragments/en404}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Two opposite diseases are given two opposite remedies, and the same Christ is the medicine for both. \emph{When we are cold in prayer} — remember the Throne, the Appearing, the Intercession, which are the consoling things. \emph{When we teem with affection and with evil concupiscence} — never forget the dread and terrible judgement-seat, and let \emph{the sound of the last trump} sound unceasingly in the ears. Comfort against coldness, terror against heat, and the prescription is symmetrical down to its clause-structure. A physician's page, and the parallel is the diagnosis.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,Four sins against the Spirit, and each is a different verb from a different book. \emph{Quench} is 1 Thessalonians v. 19 · \emph{strive against} is Stephen's \emph{ye do always resist the Holy Ghost}, Acts vii. 51 · \emph{grieve} is Ephesians iv. 30 · \emph{do despite} is Hebrews x. 29, \emph{hath done despite unto the Spirit of grace}. A reader with only the English will hear a rhetorical heap where the plate has four distinct scriptural offences, gathered from four books and set in ascending order of gravity. None is a synonym for another.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 405 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{405}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{405}{\input{fragments/la405}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{405}
\setnoted{6,13}
\enleafn{405}{\input{fragments/en405}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The communion of saints is opened out into four things, and only the first of them is people. \emph{Holy persons, actions, prayers, liturgies} — the fellowship is with acts and rites as much as with men, which is the wider of the two senses the phrase has always carried, and the page takes it by enumerating rather than by arguing. Note also that the line above hangs \emph{Catholica} at the head of its own line, where the Latin has it agreeing with the Church — \emph{in thy Catholic Church}, not "called Catholic." The plate's lineation is kept and the sense is given here.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The faith asked for is defined by four counterfeits before a single positive word, and every one of the four is a New Testament controversy. Not dead — James ii. 17 · not for a time — the believers of Luke viii. 13, who \emph{for a while believe} · not hypocritical — the \emph{faith unfeigned} of 1 Timothy i. 5 · not destroying the Law — Romans iii. 31, \emph{do we then make void the law through faith? God forbid.} Only then the positive, and it is Galatians and James together: \emph{working by love}, \emph{working together with works}. A section that opened by confessing unbelief closes by ruling out the four ways of believing wrongly — and the Creed it has run three times is left standing on a faith that must be shown to be alive.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 406 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{406}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{406}{\input{fragments/gr406}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{406}
\setnoted{2,3,23}
\enleafn{406}{\input{fragments/en406}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The confession is an anatomy, not a list of sins. After the origin — \emph{conceived in unclean seed}, \emph{warmed in iniquity in my mother's womb} — the accusation goes down the body in order: heart, mouth, lips, tongue, eyes, ears, forehead, neck, hands, feet. Ten members, each with its own text, and no deed named anywhere: what is confessed is not what the man did but what he is made of. The scripture band is empty on this leaf by decision — the plate prints a reference against almost every line and our English keeps it there, so a tag beneath would repeat the line above it (§3a).\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The reference here is wrong, and the volume corrects it eighty-three pages earlier. \emph{That I was conceived in unclean seed} wants Job xiv. 4 — \emph{who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one} — where the plate prints xiv. 14, which is \emph{if a man die, shall he live again?} Printed 323 cites the same verse rightly, as Job xiv. 4. The corroborating witness is the book itself, and both places stand as printed.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{iii}\,The whole inventory is concluded out of a single verse, split in two. \emph{Whatsoever I have done is either a spider's web, or a cockatrice' egg} — both halves are Isaiah lix. 5, and the plate's \emph{Ibid.} on the second is what shows it. The two images are not a doubling but a division: the web is what is futile, woven and clothing nobody; the egg is what is lethal, and hatches. Every work is one or the other, and there is no third case.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§2 \emph{Confessio Peccatorum}}
% ---------- printed 407 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{407}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§2 \emph{Confessio Peccatorum}}
\originalsone{407}{\input{fragments/la407}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{407}
\setnoted{14,19}
\enleafn{407}{\input{fragments/en407}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Jeremiah's landscape of idolatry is turned inward and made the man's own. \emph{Upon every green field, under every leafy tree} is the prophets' standing phrase for the high places, where the nation's whoredoms were committed — here it locates his own sins, so that the ground the idols stood on is himself. The figure beside it works the same way: \emph{as a fountain its waters, so my heart its sins} — not a man who sins but a spring that cannot help it.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The page's argument is a hardening in three stages, and each stage has its own proof-text. First into a habit — \emph{scarlet} (Isaiah i. 18, the dye that will not wash) and \emph{sold} (Ahab, who \emph{sold himself to work wickedness}, and Paul \emph{sold under sin}). Then into a nature — the leopard's spots and the Ethiopian's skin, Jeremiah's two things that cannot be changed. Then the third stage, which has no image because there is nothing left to compare it to: \emph{until I am myself not a sinner, but sin} — sealed with Micah i. 5, where the prophet does not say Samaria has sinned but that Samaria is the sin. Act, habit, nature, identity: the English keeps the four steps distinct and lets none blur into the next.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 408 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{408}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{408}{\input{fragments/la408}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{408}
\setnoted{1,12}
\enleafn{408}{\input{fragments/en408}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Sin is measured here, and the measures are all physical. \emph{Broad · hard · great in quantity · long, from my mother's breasts · thick, cords of iniquity · deep · heavy as a burden, as lead} — seven magnitudes, each with its text, and the reader should notice the plate has now moved its references out of the line and into a column down the left margin, where before they ran inline. The series then breaks its own pattern: the last item is not an eighth measure but a sound — \emph{reaching to heaven itself by their cry}. What could not be measured any further is heard instead.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The aggravations are each headed \emph{Quia}, because, and they mount to one that cannot be exceeded. Because \emph{for nothing, for vanities} · because \emph{for a handful of barley, for a morsel of bread} · because with greediness · because \emph{with a hard forehead} · because \emph{to the offence of others} · because ungrateful · \emph{the sow to her wallowing} — and then the last and shortest: \emph{Quia Christianus}, because a Christian, under Galatians ii. 21, \emph{I do not frustrate the grace of God}. The heaviest aggravation in the catalogue is two words long, and it is the only one that is not a description of the sin but of the sinner.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 409 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{409}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{409}{\input{fragments/la409}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{409}
\setnoted{1,23}
\enleafn{409}{\input{fragments/en409}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,This leaf carries two wrong references, and the volume gives the right reading for both of them elsewhere. \emph{My days are consumed in vanity, and my years in anguish of heart} stands here under Psal. xl. 9; the verse is Ps. lxxviii. 33, and printed 25 cites that same half-verse correctly. The second is at the foot of the page (see below). Both are kept as printed. The corroborating witness in each case is this book, three hundred and eighty pages apart, which is a stronger warrant than any conjecture and is why neither is mended.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The second twin of §37, and it differs from its Part II fellow twice over. The chapter figure reads Is. xxxiii. 15 — \emph{he that walketh righteously}, which is the opposite of what the line wants. The verse is Hezekiah's, Isaiah xxxviii. 15, and printed 372–373 cites it rightly. And the sentence itself has changed. Both recensions turn the Vulgate's \emph{cum ipse fecerit} — when He hath done it — into \emph{fecerim}, when I have; but §37 stammers it, \emph{fecerim, fecerim, fecerim}, three times and with no object, where here it is said once and given one: \emph{cum ipse hæc fecerim}. Where Part II could not get past the word, Part III names the thing done. Neither recension is conformed to the other, and the triple stands as a triple there.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 410 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{410}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{410}{\input{fragments/la410}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{410}
\setnoted{12,23}
\enleafn{410}{\input{fragments/en410}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,An appeal is lodged from God to God, and it is a formal legal act. \emph{I appeal therefore, O Lord, from Thee unto Thee} — \emph{from Thee the just, unto Thee the merciful · from the seat of justice, unto the throne of grace · from Thee the judge, unto Thee the Father in Christ.} The court appealed from and the court appealed to are the same court, and what makes the appeal lie is not a second judge but the Incarnation: it is \emph{the Father in Christ} who receives it. The forensic habit runs through the whole book — the \emph{Allegatio} of §7, the \emph{Interpellatio} of §32, the Areopagus at 386 — but this is the boldest of them, and the English keeps the legal words as legal words.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The ground of that appeal is God's own stated will, cited back to Him. \emph{Who wilt have all men to be saved} (1 Timothy ii. 4) and \emph{who wilt have no man perish} (2 Peter iii. 9) are set as a pair — two declarations of what God wills, entered as evidence against His justice and in favour of His mercy. The line above them is the disciples' \emph{carest thou not that we perish?}, printed under Marc. iv. 28; the verse is iv. 38, and the volume cites it rightly at printed 286 and again at 294. Kept as printed, the third such figure in two leaves.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 411 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{411}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{411}{\input{fragments/la411}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{411}
\setnoted{1,17}
\enleafn{411}{\input{fragments/en411}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The first plea is a chain of titles, and every one of them is conceded before it is held onto. \emph{A servant, and a waster, yet a servant} · \emph{bought with the price of the blood of Thy Son} · \emph{though a naughty son, and a prodigal, yet a son for all that} · \emph{though I have lost the free birth of a son, yet Thou hast not lost the pity of a Father.} The form is the same each time — the accusation admitted in full, and the relation held anyway — and it is what keeps the page from being either self-excusing or despairing.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,And then the plea leaves the man's account altogether and rests on God's property. \emph{Spare Thine own work, spare Thine own Name, spare the price of Thine own blood — if Thou wilt not spare us.} The last clause concedes the whole case and asks anyway, on the ground that the thing to be destroyed belongs to the one destroying it. What is at stake is stated as God's loss, not the sinner's, which is the argument the three preceding titles were laid down for.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 412 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{412}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{412}{\input{fragments/la412}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{412}
\setnoted{1,11}
\enleafn{412}{\input{fragments/en412}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,A brace pairs three names with three properties, and the pairing is the argument. \emph{Dust · Wind · Flesh} stand against \emph{frail · light · dissolved} — each noun answered by what it cannot help being, so the confession of what he is made of doubles as the reason he cannot be held to account for it. The two texts beneath press it: \emph{Thou wilt not pursue the stubble} is Job's, addressed to God; \emph{wilt Thou chase a flea?} is David's, addressed to Saul. A word spoken to a king is here spoken to God, which is this book's habit and is done without a mark.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,Three human kings are entered as precedents binding upon God, and the argument mounts to the worst of them. David spared Shimei who cursed him — \emph{and David was a man after Thine own heart}, so the standard is one God set himself. Then the kings of Israel, who \emph{are merciful} — which is not Israel's estimate of them but Ben-hadad's servants', a pagan's reckoning quoted with approval, and answered \emph{is there any King of Israel more merciful than Thou?} And last, Ahab — \emph{who had sold himself unto sin} — \emph{Thou didst spare him when he humbled himself, spare me also.} The final plea is that God should not do less for this man than He once did for Ahab.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 413 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{413}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{413}{\input{fragments/la413}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{413}
\setnoted{4,17}
\enleafn{413}{\input{fragments/en413}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Having appealed away from the judgement seat, he sets one up himself. \emph{But I judge myself · I think upon it again · I pronounce the sentence · I take vengeance myself upon myself}. This is the other half of the appeal at 410: justice was asked to stand aside there, and here the man supplies it in his own person, so that nothing is asked to be waived, only moved. \emph{If we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged} was quoted at printed 386 as a counsel; here it is an act performed — the same verse twice over and never for the same thing. Note the plate cites it there as 1 Cor. xi. 31 and here as xi. 30; the volume gives its own right figure, and both stand as printed.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The plea changes hands here and becomes Moses'. \emph{Shall the enemy upbraid Thee, that Thou didst create us to slay us … or because Thou canst not save?} is the argument from Numbers xiv — what the Egyptians will say — and it is joined to Joshua's and to the psalmist's \emph{the enemy hath reproached the Lord}. What is offered is no longer the sinner's need but God's standing among those who are watching. \emph{Remember what my substance is} returns here as well: the fifth place in this volume for Psalm lxxxix, and in none of the five is it doing the same work.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 414 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{414}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{414}{\input{fragments/la414}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{414}
\setnoted{1,8}
\enleafn{414}{\input{fragments/en414}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,This line is a cento of three places in Job, and it passes through three different texts of them without a mark. \emph{The infant of one day} is Job xiv. 4 \textbf{as the Septuagint reads it} — \emph{not one, even if his life be but one day upon the earth} — which the Vulgate does not say at all, its verse asking only who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean. Andrewes uses the phrase in his own voice in a Pentecost sermon and names his authority there: \emph{infans unius diei super terram}, \textup{as the Seventy read it}. Augustine had given it in the same Latin, \emph{nec infans cuius est unius diei vita super terram}. The middle clause is Vulgate verbatim and from another chapter — Job xxv. 5, \emph{stellæ non sunt mundæ in conspectu ejus}, with \emph{ipsæ} added and \emph{ejus} turned to \emph{Tuo}. The last clause is Job iv. 18 and is not the Vulgate either: that reads \emph{in angelis suis reperit pravitatem}, found depravity, where this has \emph{respexisti insipientiam}, folly, which is the Hebrew's word and the Authorised Version's. Whether he took it from a Latin made out of the Hebrew or turned it himself is not settled. The plate's figure covers none of the three: Job xxv. 3 is \emph{is there any number of his armies?} Kept as printed. Brightman's margin supplies the two outer references and none for the stars. And Job xiv. 4 is the verse this book cites rightly at printed 323 and misnumbers at 406 as xiv. 14 — quarried here a third time, with no page marking the other two.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,Three questions, and each asks what God himself stands to lose. \emph{What wilt Thou do unto that great Name of Thine?} is Joshua's after the defeat at Ai · \emph{what unto those riches of Thy mercy?} · \emph{what unto the blood of Thy Son? Shall He die for nought?} That last is Galatians ii. 21 — the very verse that six leaves back was the heaviest charge against him, where sinning \emph{because a Christian} frustrated the grace of God. Here the same text is turned round and pleads for him. Never the same work twice, and the two places do not refer to one another.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 415 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{415}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{415}{\input{fragments/la415}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{415}
\setnoted{1,13}
\enleafn{415}{\input{fragments/en415}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Four texts in a row make one argument, and it is an argument from God's own loss. \emph{What profit is there in my blood?} · \emph{shall any in death give Thee thanks?} · \emph{shall Thy wondrous works be known in the dark?} · \emph{the grave shall not confess Thee, neither shall Death praise Thee.} A dead man cannot praise, so the praise is what God forfeits by killing him — the same reckoning as the three questions at 414, now made out of the Psalter alone. It closes on the one thing the dead cannot say: \emph{the living, the living, he shall confess Thee, as I do this day.}\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,Goodness is divided into three, and the division exists so that its worst class can be claimed. \emph{Good to the good and to them that deserve well · gracious to strangers and to them that deserve nothing · merciful to the evil, and to them that deserve ill}. Then, in five words, the whole use of the taxonomy: \emph{Upon this last I take my stand.} He has sorted God's kindnesses in order to put himself in the lowest bin and claim it as his own — and the ground offered is not desert but its absence: \emph{when for no man's sake Thou canst, when for nothing's sake, for Thine own sake Thou forgivest sins.}}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 416 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{416}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{416}{\input{fragments/la416}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{416}
\setnoted{5,9}
\enleafn{416}{\input{fragments/en416}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Punishing is made God's \emph{strange} work and mercy His own. Isaiah and Habakkuk are cited \emph{to call it Thine own work to shew mercy: as though to punish and to chastise were a strange work, and abhorrent from Thy disposition} — Isaiah's own phrase for it, \emph{his strange work, his strange act}. The asymmetry is doctrinal, not rhetorical: mercy belongs to God's nature and judgement is something He is put to.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The witnesses are climbed in numbered steps, and the last step is nature — but not left standing alone. The law (7), the prophets (8), and then \emph{nature itself persuaded Job of this} — immediately qualified, \emph{by the leading of Thy Spirit}, so that even the argument from nature is referred back to grace. And the text chosen answers the leaf before it. At 413 Job ix. 3 was the impossibility of reply — \emph{not one of a thousand} could answer God. Here Job xxxiii. 23 makes \emph{one of a thousand} an angel who answers for him, and says \emph{Deliver him … for I have found wherein I may be gracious.} The same phrase, twice, and never the same work.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§3 \emph{Misericordia Dei}}
% ---------- printed 417 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{417}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§3 \emph{Misericordia Dei}}
\originalsone{417}{\input{fragments/la417}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{417}
\setnoted{2,17}
\enleafn{417}{\input{fragments/en417}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Mercy is measured, and this is the third time the volume reaches for measurement — but not with the same measures. Printed 315 took Paul's \emph{length, breadth, depth} to measure a wound, and 319 took the same three to measure mercy. Here breadth and depth return, height is added — \emph{unto the heavens}, then \emph{above the heavens} — and length is made time: \emph{everlasting, before and after}. Then the two things measured against: \emph{over our sin} (Romans v. 20) and \emph{over His own justice} (James ii. 13, where mercy \emph{rejoiceth against judgment}). The second is the harder claim and the page makes it without argument.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,Mercy is not an attribute God has but a name God is, and the point is made by citation rather than argument. \emph{Natural unto Him} · \emph{Mercy itself is called God} · Augustine's \emph{O Name, under which no man may despair} · Chrysostom's \emph{great is the gulf of my sins, but greater is the deep of the mercy of God.} The two fathers are set to answer the two things the section has been afraid of — the name that forbids despair, and a depth measured against the gulf just confessed.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 418 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{418}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{418}{\input{fragments/la418}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{418}
\setnoted{1,13}
\enleafn{418}{\input{fragments/en418}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Four near-synonyms are braced together, and the point of the brace is that they are not quite synonyms. \emph{Patient · Longsuffering · Slow to anger · Long refraining Himself} — the last is not a temper but an act, something God does to God. Beneath them the Vulgate's \emph{dissimulas}: God \emph{winking at} the sins of men, that they may repent — a pretence of not seeing, held for the sake of the outcome.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,Judgement is folded inside mercy rather than set against it. \emph{Not even His judgment is void of mercy} — and then the sentence the whole head turns on: \emph{The punishment is a part of the mercy}, with the psalm's \emph{I will visit their offences with the rod, yet My mercy will I not take from him}. Two leaves back the argument was the opposite way about, where punishing was God's \emph{strange work} and foreign to His disposition (416). Here it is not foreign but instrumental, and \emph{for a great sin a little punishment sufficeth a father}. Neither statement is qualified by the other, and the book leaves both standing.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 419 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{419}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{419}{\input{fragments/la419}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{419}
\setnoted{13,20}
\enleafn{419}{\input{fragments/en419}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Here, in its own words and its own tense, is the verse this book everywhere turns into a command. \emph{David said, I have sinned, O Lord. Nathan answered, The Lord also hath put away thy sin, thou shalt not die.} It is an indicative, and it is somebody else's — a prophet's word to a king, reported as narrative. Elsewhere the volume takes exactly this sentence and prays it back as \emph{Transfer}, put thou away; here it is left standing as the thing that was said. A reader who has crossed Part II will recognise the raw material of the book's commonest movement, printed once in the state it was found in.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The fourth property of mercy is \emph{fellow-suffering}, and it is not softened. \emph{Though we deserve it, yet He grieveth with us in our calamity} — and the name for it is Zacharias' \emph{tender bowels of His mercy}, the \emph{viscera misericordiæ}, which is an organ and not a sentiment. The close answers a concession made eight leaves back: at 411 the plea had granted that \emph{God heareth not sinners} — John ix. 31, in the mouth of the man born blind. Here: \emph{who not only heareth sinners, but also, in the day of their trouble, those who in the time of their peace despised Him.} The objection is not argued down; it is simply outlived.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 420 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{420}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{420}{\input{fragments/la420}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{420}
\setnoted{7,17}
\enleafn{420}{\input{fragments/en420}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Two fathers take back two sons, and the pardons are deliberately unequal. David brought Absalom back — \emph{yet at the first that he should not see his face, and at the last admitted him to the kiss}: a pardon in stages, with the face withheld. The prodigal's father \emph{not only forgave him, but made ready the best robe and the ring, and the fatted calf} — everything at once, and nothing withheld. The head being illustrated is \emph{lavish} pardon, so the first example stands as the measure the second exceeds.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The law is quoted in full and then overruled by the lawgiver, and the contradiction is left on the page. Jeremiah states the rule and its inescapable answer: a wife put away who \emph{become another man's} is defiled — \emph{shall she return unto him again?} Deuteronomy says she shall not. Then, without a word of reconciliation: \emph{but thou hast played the harlot with many lovers; yet return again unto Me, saith the Lord.} The list beneath it climbs by the same logic — \emph{the disciples that forsook Him, Peter that forswore Him, the thief that blasphemed, and the Jews that crucified Him} — each pardon harder than the last, and the series stops only at the worst case it can name.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 421 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{421}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{421}{\input{fragments/la421}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{421}
\setnoted{1,11}
\enleafn{421}{\input{fragments/en421}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Grace is given three motions in a brace, and the three are a doctrine in three words. \emph{Preventing} — going before, the \emph{gratia præveniens} of the schools · \emph{Following} · \emph{Compassing about}, \emph{on every side}. Before, behind and around, so that no approach is left for the man to have made himself: the sequence forecloses the question of who moved first.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,God is said to have \emph{learned} mercy, and to be practised in it. \emph{He is merciful not by nature only, but by practice … He hath learned to shew mercy, and hath had the practice of it from of old.} The numbered heads are climbing a ladder of grounds — nature, then practice, then promise, then Christ — and each is meant to be harder to doubt than the last. The denials beneath are three prophetic figures for a God grown incapable, all refused: not \emph{a spring dried up}, not \emph{a hand shortened}, not \emph{an ear made heavy}.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 422 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{422}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{422}{\input{fragments/la422}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{422}
\setnoted{6,21}
\enleafn{422}{\input{fragments/en422}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Three men who would not take back a word, and the argument gains force as the witnesses lose worth. \emph{If Isaac would not change his word} — the blessing got by fraud, \emph{yea, and he shall be blessed} · \emph{if the Persian would not, a heathen} — Darius, bound by the law of the Medes against his own friend · \emph{if profane Pilate would not} — \emph{what I have written I have written.} Then: \emph{Surely God never will.} The series descends in dignity while ascending in strength, and ends on the man who condemned Christ. It is the same move as the appeal to Ahab at 412: the argument is strongest where the example is worst.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The plea is that one memory must not drive out another. Augustine: \emph{Lord, look not so upon my sin that Thou shouldest therefore forget Thine own Name.} And the Name is not incidental to the argument — \emph{Jesu, this is His name, because He saveth us from our sins}, so that to remember the Name is already to have granted the request. Shimei returns here from printed 412, where David sparing him was offered as a precedent; now it is the title that carries it — \emph{Son of David}, who forgave Shimei … do Thou also forgive.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 423 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{423}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{423}{\input{fragments/la423}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{423}
\setnoted{4,26}
\enleafn{423}{\input{fragments/en423}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The apostles are called as witnesses in a numbered series, and one of them is never announced. \emph{Thine Apostle} is Paul, then \emph{the second Apostle} is Peter, then \emph{the fourth} is John — but James stands between them, quoted and not counted: \emph{mercy rejoiceth against judgment}, in its place in the order and without a heading of its own. Reported as it stands; nothing is supplied.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The last witness called is Christ himself, and the series was built to end there. \emph{Nor in vain shalt Thou Thyself have said, Come unto Me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden.} After the apostles, the one they were witnesses to — and the tense is the point: \emph{shalt Thou have said}, so that the whole chain of quotations is set as evidence of something that would be void if the invitation failed. The figure printed against it is Matt. xi. 25, where the words are xi. 28; kept as printed.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 424 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{424}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{424}{\input{fragments/la424}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{424}
\setnoted{3,14}
\enleafn{424}{\input{fragments/en424}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The verdict clause of the whole argument, and then the turn from proving to asking. \emph{These things were not said in vain, they cannot be} — everything quoted since 415 has been entered as evidence, and this is the finding upon it. Three \emph{wherefores} then mark the change of business: \emph{wherefore … these Thy comforts have refreshed my soul} · \emph{wherefore let us come boldly unto the throne of grace} · \emph{now therefore hear, O Lord.} The case rested, the petition begins, and the throne appealed to is the one named at 410.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,Twenty leaves of argument end on the shortest prayer in the Gospels. \emph{God be merciful to me a sinner} — the publican's seven words, reached only after the law, the prophets, nature, the apostles and Christ have each been called. The disproportion is the point: the whole apparatus was built to earn the right to say the one sentence that needed none of it.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 425 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{425}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{425}{\input{fragments/gr425}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{425}
\setnoted{9,14}
\enleafn{425}{\input{fragments/en425}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The catena tags each blessing with whose it was, and one of the tags does not fit its text. \emph{Blessed be the God of Jethro} is exact — Exodus xviii. 10 is Jethro's own blessing. But \emph{Let us sing unto the Lord of Isaac and of the Israelites} is Exodus xv. 2, the song at the Red Sea, which is Moses' and Israel's, and Isaac has no part in it. Whether the name is a compositor's slip, a scribe's, or a compression of something else cannot be settled, and nothing is claimed here. Transcribed as printed and left as a question.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,Four apostolic blessings are set in a row and three of them open with the same words. \emph{Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ} stands three times — from 1 Peter, from Ephesians, from 2 Corinthians — with Zacharias' \emph{Blessed be the Lord God of Israel} set among them. The repetition is not accidental and is not reduced: one formula, four grounds — a new birth, a spiritual blessing, a visitation, and comfort in tribulation.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§4 \emph{Gratiarum Actio}}
% ---------- printed 426 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{426}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§4 \emph{Gratiarum Actio}}
\originalsone{426}{\input{fragments/la426}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{426}
\setnoted{1,20}
\enleafn{426}{\input{fragments/en426}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The thanksgiving begins before birth, and it is the exact counterpart of the confession at 406. Psalm cxxxix and Job x are laid together to make one embryology: \emph{my substance in the lower parts of the earth} · \emph{Thine eyes did see my imperfection} · \emph{Thou hast milked me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese} · \emph{clothed me with skin and flesh, and fenced me with bones and sinews.} Printed 406 began at the same place — \emph{conceived in unclean seed, warmed in iniquity in my mother's womb} — and then went down the body member by member. The same body is catalogued twice in this Part, once as filth and once as workmanship, and neither page mentions the other.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,Jacob is here for the third time in this volume, and each time it is a different clause of the same night. Here it is his prayer before meeting Esau — \emph{I am not worthy of all Thy mercies … with my staff I passed over this Jordan, and now I return with two bands}, the whole of a life measured by what he set out with. At 422 it was \emph{I will not let Thee go, except Thou bless me}; at printed 375 the wrestling was turned into a refusal — \emph{give me another Thee; else will I not let Thee go.} One night at the ford, quarried three times and never for the same thing.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 427 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{427}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{427}{\input{fragments/la427}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{427}
\setnoted{3,18}
\enleafn{427}{\input{fragments/en427}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,One wrong numeral here drags four more references after it. The line above is rightly \emph{Psal. ciii. 1}; this one is printed \emph{cxiii. 2} — but \emph{forget not all His benefits} is Psalm ciii. 2, and so are the four verses beneath it, which the plate cites by bare figure alone (\emph{3 · 4 · 5}) and which therefore hang from the wrong psalm. Five references, one slip. And the volume gives cxiii. 2 correctly on the very next leaf, at 428, for \emph{Blessed be the Name of the Lord from this time forth} — which is what that psalm does say. All kept as printed.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The thanksgiving is made almost entirely out of other men's words. From here to the end of the leaf there is scarcely a clause that is not the Psalter's, and the plate marks the continuations by bare verse-figure — \emph{ver. 19 · 21 · 22} — so that whole psalms are walked up rather than quoted from. The one image worth halting on is a resurrection borrowed for a life: \emph{Thou … broughtest me from the deep of the earth again.}}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 428 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{428}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{428}{\input{fragments/la428}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{428}
\setnoted{6,16}
\enleafn{428}{\input{fragments/en428}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The doxology is compiled out of four separate visions, and it is longer than any of them. \emph{Glory, honour, blessing, power, Godhead, wisdom, might, dominion, salvation, love, thanksgiving, praise} — drawn from Revelation iv, v, vii and xix, whose ascriptions each carry seven terms or fewer. No one company in heaven says all of this; the page gathers what the four said separately and offers it \emph{unto the holy and undivided Trinity}. The heavenly liturgy is compiled, not quoted.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The list of benefits begins at bare existence and works outward, and its first three steps are metaphysical before they are social. \emph{That I am · I live · endued with reason} — being, then life, then mind, which is the old ladder of the soul — and only then \emph{a citizen, a Christian, free, free-born, of an honest stock}. Nothing is too fundamental to be thanked for, and the first item on the list is that there is anybody to make it.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 429 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{429}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{429}{\input{fragments/la429}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{429}
\setnoted{1,9}
\enleafn{429}{\input{fragments/en429}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Three kinds of good, and the third has no classical counterpart. \emph{Of nature, of fortune, of grace} — the first two are the philosophers' division of what a man may possess, and grace is added as a third that no philosopher could have supplied. The form of the pagan scheme is kept and its sufficiency denied, in three words and without argument.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,God's acts and the man's own responses are thanked for in one undivided list. \emph{Redemption, Regeneration, Catechizing, Calling} — and then, in the same brace and on the same footing, \emph{Thy Patience} beside \emph{My Compunction}, with \emph{the hope of pardon} and \emph{if we do anything well} after them. His own repentance is counted among the gifts received, not offered as something brought — which is why the possessives can sit next to each other without a seam. The English keeps them adjacent and keeps both capitals.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 430 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{430}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{430}{\input{fragments/la430}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{430}
\setnoted{2,12}
\enleafn{430}{\input{fragments/en430}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Seven channels of benefit are braced together, and the last one is not like the others. \emph{Writings · Sermons · Discourse · Prayers · Examples · Reproof · Injuries} — thanks is rendered for the men who have wronged him, in the same list and on the same footing as those who taught him, and the plate makes no distinction between them.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The page is set in three columns and the middle one carries a single word that changes. Six pairs stand opposite each other — \emph{known} / \emph{unknown} · \emph{manifest} / \emph{hidden} · \emph{which we remember} / \emph{which we forget}, then \emph{I confess} / \emph{I will confess} · \emph{I bless} / \emph{I will bless} · \emph{I give thanks} / \emph{I will give thanks}. The word between them is \emph{or} through the first three and \emph{and} through the last. The switch is where the page turns from what was received to what is rendered: the benefits are alternatives, of which some are hidden — but the thanks are cumulative, present \emph{and} future both. The middle column is doing grammar, not decoration, and must survive into both layers.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 431 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{431}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{431}{\input{fragments/gr431}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{431}
\setnoted{6,21}
\enleafn{431}{\input{fragments/en431}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The book's last section returns to its first argument. \emph{At evening, and morning, and at noonday will I pray} is the psalm the volume opened on at printed 2, where the canonical hours were built out of Scripture — a text found for each hour at which somebody in Scripture is praying — rather than inherited from a breviary. Four hundred pages later the hours are simply kept, without the argument, which is what it looks like when a case has been made and is being lived on.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,Isaiah's promise is prayed back as a command for the third time in this volume, and here it is fitted to the hour. God says \emph{I have blotted out thy transgressions as a cloud}; the prayer answers \emph{Blot out, O Lord, as the cloud of night our iniquities, and as the morning mist our sins.} The cloud has become a night cloud and the mist a morning one — the figure adapted to the office it is being said at. The same verse stands at printed 22 already turned into a petition, and at printed 332 in God's own indicative, untouched. Three settings, and no page marks the other two.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§5 \emph{Matutinæ Preces}}
% ---------- printed 432 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{432}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§5 \emph{Matutinæ Preces}}
\originalsone{432}{\input{fragments/la432}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{432}
\setnoted{1,21}
\enleafn{432}{\input{fragments/en432}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,One psalm is quarried across two leaves to cover the whole of a day. Psalm xci gives the night terrors on the leaf before — \emph{the terror by night}, \emph{the thing that walketh about in darkness} — and gives this leaf its daylight ones: \emph{the arrow that flieth by day}, \emph{the assault}, and \emph{the noonday devil}. That last is the Vulgate against the Prayer Book, which reads \emph{the sickness that destroyeth in the noon-day}, and is one of the places where our English follows the Latin because Andrewes did; it was the same at printed 24. Morning, noon and night out of a single psalm.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The book ends on the pair it began with, and this time the reference is right. \emph{Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth} and \emph{let my speech be with grace, seasoned with salt} stood together in the same order at printed 26, near the volume's opening. There the plate cited the psalm as cxli. 8, where the words are verse 3; here it prints cxli. 3. The volume corrects itself across four hundred leaves, and both figures stand as printed.}
\clearpage
\sethead{§6 \emph{Vespertinæ Preces}}
% ---------- printed 433 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{433}
\setnoted{}
\addcontentsline{toc}{section}{§6 \emph{Vespertinæ Preces}}
\originalsone{433}{\input{fragments/la433}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{433}
\setnoted{7,23}
\enleafn{433}{\input{fragments/en433}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Two references on this leaf are right only on the Prayer Book's numbering, and that is the hardest evidence in the volume about which Psalter was physically on the desk. \emph{The Lord hath granted His loving-kindness in the day-time} is cited xlii. 10, and \emph{the outgoings of the morning and of the evening} lxv. 8 — figures that answer in the Coverdale Psalter and not in the Authorised Version. Everywhere else the question is settled by wording, which can be remembered; here it is settled by a numeral, which has to be looked up. Somebody had the Prayer Book open.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,Hezekiah's psalm returns for the evening office, and it is being thanked rather than prayed. \emph{Who hast not cut off, like a weaver, our life, nor from the morning even unto the evening made an end of us} — the sick king's \emph{I have cut off like a weaver my life}, turned from complaint into a benediction for the day survived. Isaiah xxxviii carried the whole of §37's confession and the twin at 409; here it does a third thing, and none of the three places refers to the others.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 434 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{434}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{434}{\input{fragments/la434}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{434}
\setnoted{1,8}
\enleafn{434}{\input{fragments/en434}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The Gospel's measure of forgiveness is taken over to count sins instead. \emph{Seven times in the day the just man stumbleth} is Proverbs — \emph{but we (miserable sinners) seventy times seven}. At printed 377 that figure was what God was required to forgive, and the page there multiplied it out to four hundred and ninety to make the demand exact. Here the same number counts the falls. The measure of mercy has become the measure of need, and neither page mentions the other.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,A precept given to men is turned round and prayed to God. \emph{Let not the sun go down upon your wrath} is Paul's rule for the Ephesians' quarrels; here it is \emph{let not the sun go down upon Thy wrath}. The command is God's own, given back to Him as a petition — and at the evening office the sun going down is not a figure but the hour the prayer is being said at. The English keeps the second person and does not soften it into a wish.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 435 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{435}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{435}{\input{fragments/la435}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{435}
\setnoted{6,25}
\enleafn{435}{\input{fragments/en435}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,The examination of conscience is carried on into unconsciousness. \emph{Let my sleep be, as a rest from labour, so a rest from sin} — and then further in: \emph{let me think nothing, even in my dreams, that may offend Thee, or defile me.} Sleep is asked for as a moral condition and not merely a bodily one, which is where §41's evening \emph{Scrutinium} was always heading; the search does not stop when the searcher does.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,One line said twice with a single word changed, and the book turns on it. \emph{By the lamp burning, to see Thee · By the lamp quenched, to see Thee.} The lamp put out is the bedside candle and it is also the life, and the next lines say so plainly — \emph{the long sleep, the sleep of death, the bed of the sepulchre.} The petition is identical on both sides because the request does not change when the light does.}
\clearpage
% ---------- printed 436 ----------
\versoalign
\markright{436}
\setnoted{}
\originalsone{436}{\input{fragments/la436}}{}
\clearpage
\markright{436}
\setnoted{1,3}
\enleafn{436}{\input{fragments/en436}}{}{\textsuperscript{i}\,Four names for the grave, and every one of them is a bed. \emph{The long sleep · the sleep of death · the bed of the sepulchre · the litter of worms · the covering of dust} — the figure begun at the pillow is carried all the way down and never changed for another.\\[1pt]\textsuperscript{ii}\,The book ends on the sentence a man says going to sleep and says dying, and it has said it once before. \emph{In peace, in the selfsame, will I sleep and take my rest} is the Compline psalm, \emph{in idipsum}; and the last words of all are \emph{Into Thy hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit, for Thou hast redeemed me}. That verse stood at printed 26, among the morning prayers, where the plate cited it on the Prayer Book's numbering. The volume opens its day and closes its life with one sentence, and the lamp two lines above has just made the two the same act. Nothing on either page marks the return.}
\clearpage
